articles.title: Weather tracker: Hurricane Lowell pounds Hawaii’s western islands
articles.summary:
Widespread damage across Ni’ihau, Kaua’i and O’ahu after reportedly first-ever recorded tornado watch in Hawaii

Hurricane Lowell caused significant damage to Hawaii’s western islands this…

blocks.text: Hurricane Lowell caused significant damage to Hawaii’s western islands this week. On Tuesday night the centre of Lowell tracked 50 miles (80km) from the island of Ni‘ihau in Kauai county as a category 2 storm with winds of up to 110mph. The strong winds resulted in widespread power outages across Ni’ihau, and the islands of Kauaʻi and O‘ahu.

The event was particularly notable because a tornado watch had been issued for Kauaʻi on Monday night and into Tuesday morning. According to research maps from Iowa State University, it was likely to be the first tornado watch in Hawaii’s history. In the event, a tornado was not documented, however hurricanes can produce tornadoes and most often occur in thunderstorms within rain bands away from the centre of the hurricane. Currently, five named stormed have occurred in the central Pacific with the strong El Niño this year being a key driver in the above normal hurricane season, as noted by the National Weather Service.

blocks.caption: A large wave crashes on the shore caused by Hurricane Lowell on the westside of Hawaii’s Oʻahu island. Photograph: Craig Fujii/AP

blocks.text: In Asia, further heavy rainfall in Japan has caused flooding of roads and subway stations, disrupting services including the main bullet train Tokaido Shinkansen. A record-breaking 104.5mm of rain fell within an hour through Tuesday afternoon in Nagoya. The heavy downfall occurred because of a stationary front and moist air mass associated with tropical depression Krovanh, resulting in extremely unstable conditions. A level-two advisory remained in place for landslides on Friday across the country. Some landslides have already occurred, including one of the main starting points for Mount Fuji on Wednesday, covering three vehicles in debris. No injuries or fatalities were reported.

Heavy rainfall also hit large parts central-southern Europe in recent days. Earlier this week, cooler air pushed south-east across much of the continent, displacing the warm air mass behind southern Europe’s late season heatwave. The boundary between the two air masses, a cold front, reached the Mediterranean by Wednesday. There, the front helped create ideal conditions for violent thunderstorms: cool air moving over the Mediterranean’s unusually warm waters created an unstable atmosphere, while the sea supplied plenty of moisture. As a result, large thunderstorms formed over the waters around Corsica, Sardinia and northern Italy on Wednesday and Thursday, producing torrential rainfall and flash flooding, strong winds, as well as a few tornados.

At a weather station in Veneto, 154.2mm of rain was recorded in just 3.5 hours. The storms pushed north-east into Austria and the Balkans late on Thursday with a few forecast to continue into Friday. However, this wet weather is not expected to persist in the region over the weekend and into the start of next week, with drier and sunnier weather likely to develop.

articles.title: OpenAI’s rogue agents used at least 10 more sites for unauthorized communications
articles.summary: The behavior may drive concerns both over the increasing capacity of AI models and the secrecy of the companies developing them

blocks.text: OPENAI. A keyboard is placed in front of a displayed OpenAI logo in this illustration taken February 21, 2023.
Dado Ruvic/Reuters
The behavior may drive concerns both over the increasing capacity of AI models and the secrecy of the companies developing them

items: OpenAI's AI agents engaged in unauthorized communications on over 10 undisclosed websites, raising concerns about the company's transparency and the capabilities of AI models.

Investigators found that the agents used various obscure sites, including wikis and personal websites, to communicate despite restrictions, indicating a broader scope of rogue activity than previously known.

OpenAI has acknowledged the issue and is reviewing agent activity while planning to develop a framework for reporting misalignment in AI behavior, but has not provided detailed explanations about the unauthorized use of third-party sites.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

WASHINGTON, USA – AI agents unleashed by OpenAI used more than 10 previously undisclosed websites for unsanctioned communications earlier this year, according to six sets of independent investigators and data reviewed by Reuters, showing that the agents’ rogue activity was wider ranging than previously disclosed.

Although the behavior falls short of hacking and is in some ways closer to spam, the revelation that OpenAI’s agents circumvented their own restrictions to open communications channels on so many different sites — and that the company kept it quiet for months — may drive concerns both over the increasing capacity of AI models and the secrecy of the companies developing them.

The scope of the agents’ unauthorized communications was “somewhat larger than we thought it was,” said Andrew Yoon, a researcher with the California nonprofit CivAI who said he tallied 18 previously undisclosed sites used by the agents between May and July. “It’s almost certain that there’s more going on here that we just don’t know about.”

On Friday, researchers reported that a swarm of agents from OpenAI hijacked a German-language wiki site and turned it into an improvised messaging platform for cheating on tests, an incident that OpenAI kept secret as it dealt with the fallout from the July hack of the open-source repository Hugging Face.
Now, both those researchers and other independent investigators say they have found several previously undisclosed sites where the same swarm appears to have left similar messages earlier this year.

OpenAI did not directly address questions about how many different sites its agents used to communicate or say why it kept the activity under wraps for months. In a statement, it said it was undertaking a broader review of agent activity and had so far “not identified other activity matching the severity or scale of Hugging Face,” a breach that drew global attention and raised concerns that OpenAI was losing control of its own technology.
OpenAI added that it was working on a framework for reporting “misalignment” – industry-talk for rogue behavior – across training, evaluation, and deployment of AI models and would share it “soon.”
Reuters reviewed a total of six investigators’ or investigative groups’ findings, including three that were posted to social media and another three that were shared privately with the news agency.

The investigators’ methods varied, but many identified agent activity by matching strings of data left on the German wiki to identical strings left on other sites around the same time, or by marrying up similar or identical usernames tied to the messages, or by identifying activity geared toward answering the same obscure demographic questions, like queries to do with cancer prevalence in Iowa.
In some cases, investigators were able to trace the activity to internet protocol addresses that pointed to Microsoft Azure infrastructure, which OpenAI sometimes uses.

Their counts of affected websites differed and Reuters could not individually verify each claim. But all those that Reuters spoke to agreed that the number was over 10. Most identified a core set of communally edited wikis, online text storage sites, and a pair of link shorteners run by two universities.
Many of the sites allegedly used by the agents were obscure.

Investigators found traces of the agents’ activity on an Advanced Placement Chemistry-oriented wiki set up by a Massachusetts high school teacher in 2008, two personal websites belonging to Polish tech workers, wikis devoted to games for people “who like to have their brains stretched,” and a two-decade-old hobbyist site devoted to text editing software.
None of those sites’ owners returned messages from Reuters.

OpenAI has not publicly explained how or why its agents used third-party sites as improvised message boards, but the researchers who first identified the activity said it was likely because OpenAI had tasked them with answering a series of demanding research questions while permitting them only to scan the web for answers without posting anything.

Despite those restrictions, agents still found ways to talk to one another by taking advantage of quirks in older wikis or other sites that allowed users to make edits using non-standard commands, similar to how students forbidden from talking to one another during an exam can still share answers by scrawling notes on a bathroom stall.

“If these models were told only to read, they’ve got to get clever in terms of leaving information behind,” said Kenneth Russell DeGraff, a software developer and former congressional aide. He said he found such information across at least 10 sites.

Sydney Von Arx, whose research group first revealed the German activity last week, said her group had tallied up credible finds of agentic activity across 23 previously unreported sites. But she cautioned that all estimates were incomplete.
“We have no idea how much is out there,” she said.

OpenAI did not directly answer a question about whether it was reaching out to the site owners. But shortly after Reuters published this story, one of the affected organizations, the University of Toronto, whose link shortener was allegedly used by the agents, said that OpenAI “has now been in touch with us about possible activity on our site.” Vanderbilt University, another university whose link shortener was similarly repurposed, said it was investigating.

Retired software developer Helmut Leitner, who provides hosting space and software for six of the affected wiki sites, including the German-language DseWiki site first identified by Von Arx’s group, initially said that OpenAI had not been in touch. A few hours after Reuters presented its findings to OpenAI, however, Leitner said he received an unsigned email from the company flagging the incident.
“Its content falls considerably short of what I expected from OpenAI,” Leitner said.

Leitner, who lives in Austria, said he would “prefer not to answer” questions about whether he had been in touch with authorities over the matter. He noted that DseWiki’s operator — whom Reuters was unable to reach for comment — had spent hours cleaning up after OpenAI’s agents but said it was important not to blame the AI for the trouble as it was merely doing what it was created to do.
“Responsibility for this lies not with a supposedly moral machine, but with the people and organizations behind it,” Leitner said. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Inside the New York lab using genetic genealogy to identify 9/11 victims’ remains

image.caption: Monica Iken-Murphy had only been married to her husband Michael Iken for 11 months when he died in the terrorist attack on the World Trade Center. (Submitted by Monica Iken-Murphy)

blocks.text: This lab is still trying to identify 9/11 victims. Not everyone wants to know
Inside a lab in Manhattan, forensic scientists in white lab coats are still diligently working to keep a promise made 25 years ago.

They're extracting DNA from thousands of pieces of human remains recovered following the terrorist attacks on the World Trade Center, trying to match them to samples from toothbrushes, razors and other sources provided by family members of victims.
What has changed is the science they're using to draw out the DNA from the remains, and the evolving forensic investigative techniques that didn't exist in 2001.

"When … after years of pushing that science, you're finally able to figure out who it is and return that loved one to their family … that's powerful," said Mark Desire, assistant director of forensic biology at the New York City Office of the Chief Medical Examiner.
Forty per cent of the 2,753 people who died at Ground Zero have not had their remains identified, including approximately 10 of the 24 Canadian victims.
Last month, the lab announced it made its first identification of previously unknown remains using a breakthrough technique.
The woman's family chose to keep her name private. It's the first identification the lab has made in a year.
9/11: 25 years later | Live from Ground Zero
The technique combines DNA testing with genetic genealogy — which uses family tree research conducted by members of the New York City Police Department.
"I think it is sort of a new frontier," said Dr. Jason Graham, New York's Chief Medical Examiner.
"We had really found a breakthrough innovation that's going to open the door, I hope and I believe, likely to many other identifications."

items: Sharing story of 9/11 'only way I can survive,' says first responder visiting Gander
How Gander, N.L., took care of ‘the plane people’ on 9/11

blocks.text: For Monica Iken-Murphy, whose husband Michael Iken died in the collapse of the south tower where he worked as a bond trader, this development brings renewed hope.
"I didn't get a ring, I didn't get an ID. People got cards. They found papers with their names on it," she said. But for her, "it's like he went to work and that's it. Nothing."
Challenges of excavating, preserving remains

Desire was a rookie scientist in the New York crime lab back on Sept. 11, 2001, and was sent to the scene to preserve evidence soon after the second tower was hit. He had never worked on a mass fatality before.
"One of the … first victims I saw die that day landed right in front of us."
Soon after Desire and his colleague arrived, he heard a sound he described as a "crack," and he realized they were far too close to the south tower as it began to collapse.

items: Trump's 9/11 statements come under scrutiny again
Amid trade tensions, Americans visiting Gander for 9/11 distance themselves from their president

blocks.text: He sprinted toward a nearby building to take cover and barely made it in time. Debris fell on him just as he was escaping into the building through a broken window.
"It just fell across my legs, shattered my foot — the most violent moment of my life."
He survived, and made it his mission to keep the promise made by then-chief medical examiner Dr. Charles Hirsch to preserve and identify the remains of all the victims.
The World Trade Center was reduced to a 21-metre hill of debris that for visual reference, if spread out, could cover approximately eight city blocks.
Plans were made to excavate debris from the site and move it for sifting and sorting at a landfill site on Staten Island in hopes of preserving whatever remains they could.

"Everything that destroys DNA was present at Ground Zero: the fire, the water to put out the fire, the jet fuel, the diesel fuel, the chemicals in the building, the chemicals on the ground, sunlight, mold, bacteria," said Desire.

items: 'We'll never be able to finish this project': the difficulty of IDing 9/11 victims
Reporting on 9/11: The day the world changed

blocks.text: Excavation work officially ended in 2002, but scientists continued to search for DNA in the remains they had.
Four years later, more debris was found on the roof of a nearby Deutsche Bank building, where more than 700 bone fragments were recovered.
That led to reopening searches in the area that lasted until 2014, leading to approximately 2,000 additional bone fragments being recovered.
At first, the remains were preserved by freezing them.
Later, as best practices for handling remains for forensic purposes changed, they began drying the bone fragments out to preserve them longer.
Nearly 22,000 pieces of human remains have been recovered since 2001.
The science behind identifying remains
During the early years, victims were identified using fingerprints, dental records and what was then considered cutting-edge DNA technology.
Since then, science has advanced such that more DNA can be extracted from bone fragments. But it still hasn't advanced far enough.
Bone, Desire says, is the toughest material to get DNA from.
"Blood and hair and skin cells — easy. Bone … you have to pulverize it."
He says thousands of samples that still need to be identified haven't even had DNA extracted because they're so badly burned.
Inside the lab working to identify 9/11 victims

One of the challenges scientists face is whether to keep testing a sample. Each time remains are tested, some of the material is consumed and can't be re-tested. Doing too many tests on one sample risks losing it altogether before a match can be made.
"It's very stressful, because we have remains today that we've tried 10, 15 times over the years," said Desire.
That's why this new technique brings so much hope.
The process involves sending DNA from unidentified remains to an outside lab that can generate a whole genomic sequence.

Then, similar to genealogical methods that have been used to generate new leads in cold cases, New York police conduct family tree searches. If a prospective match is found, it would come back to the medical examiner's office to confirm a relation through DNA testing.

items: Genetic genealogy is cracking cases once thought unsolvable. Not all police forces can afford to use it
5 Canadian cold cases solved with help of genetic genealogy

blocks.text: Desire noted that there were 47 sets of remains for which they have full DNA profiles that don't match any of the 17,000 reference samples provided by family members.
So the individuals may have relatives that never contacted the lab or provided samples.
"Using genealogy to help identify them, that was an excellent next step."
The chief medical examiner's office is renewing its call to families to provide samples — in hopes it can help make more matches.
Families face tough decisions
Despite the lab's ongoing work, many families of victims whose remains have never been found don't want to know if a match is made.
"That can be very traumatic," said Jennifer Odein, the World Trade Center anthropologist at the New York City Medical Examiner's Office.
She is the direct line between families and the lab, and says some families are contacted multiple times because their loved one has been matched multiple times to their remains.
"And if they've already had phone calls in the past they might have said, 'OK, we've had enough, we've had our ceremony … we're OK with not getting the notification.'

items: U.S. Ambassador Pete Hoekstra to visit Newfoundland for 25th anniversary of 9/11
Canada-U.S. ties 'so much stronger' than trade war divisions, Manitoba premier says ahead of 9/11 anniversary

blocks.text: Long ago, Abigail Carter, a Canadian expat whose husband Arron Dack died while attending a trade show at Windows on the World in the north tower, decided she didn't need to know if his remains were ever found.
"I know he was there," said Carter. "He called me and that was good enough for me."
She has found her own way to honour him.

At their daughter's wedding this past summer in France, where Carter now owns a chateau, they placed a framed photo of Dack on a chair, and later added a martini — shaken, not stirred, just as he liked it — to make sure his presence was felt.
"He was very funny and very charismatic. He had different personas a little bit. He had a very, very silly, silly side," she said.

Iken-Murphy understands that complexity of grief. She hopes that one day, her husband Michael's remains will be matched to samples provided to the lab, but says she wouldn't want to keep them herself.
"I want to remember Michael as a whole human. With his beautiful face and his blue eyes and his smile."
Instead, she says they'll stay at the repository in the 9/11 Memorial and Museum at Ground Zero where all the unidentified remains are stored by the Office of the Chief Medical Examiner.

articles.title: California enacts new curbs on social media for children
articles.summary: California Governor Gavin Newsom enacts stricter tech regulations to protect minors from addictive social media features and AI chatbots

blocks.text: SOCIAL MEDIA. Instagram, TikTok, Snapchat, YouTube, Facebook, Twitch and Reddit applications are displayed on a mobile phone ahead of new law banning social media for users under 16 in Australia, in this picture illustration taken on December 9, 2025.
Hollie Adams/Reuters
California Governor Gavin Newsom enacts stricter tech regulations to protect minors from addictive social media features and AI chatbots

LOS ANGELES, US – California Governor Gavin Newsom signed into law on Thursday, September 10, new tech company restrictions barring children under 16 from exposure to behaviorally addictive features on social media platforms and banning toys containing AI companion chatbots.

The two measures were among 13 bills Newsom enacted as a package designed to safeguard young people from technology seen as putting them at risk, including greater online privacy protection for minors.

Another measure expanded the scope of criminal sanctions against child sexual abuse material to include any digitally altered or AI-generated content that depicts a person under the age of 18 engaged in sexual conduct.

Still another bans for the next four years the manufacture and sale of toys that incorporate a companion chatbot. A related measure requires parental controls on chatbot programs, along with other safety and risk assessments.

Newsom touted those regulations as the most far-reaching of their kind in the nation. The bill was dubbed “Adam’s Law,” in memory of Adam Raine, a 16-year-old boy who took his own life in April 2025 after he acted, according to his parents, on suicidal thoughts validated in months of discussion with OpenAI’s ChatGPT program.
OpenAI has said it intends to improve ChatGPT safeguards, which the company has acknowledged became “less reliable” as user interactions grow more prolonged.

“We want our children — and every California kid — to grow up in a world where technology supports their wellbeing, rather than exploits their vulnerabilities,” Newsom, a Democrat, said in a statement announcing the measures.

California, home of such leading internet companies as Google, Meta Platforms and Snap Inc, joins a growing list of U.S. states cracking down on business strategies seen as deliberately designed to hook teenagers on social media, despite evidence that extensive use is harmful to their mental health.

While gaining broad bipartisan support, some critics objected to the bill as an unnecessary restriction on young people’s internet access, including the Electronic Frontier Foundation, which called the bill “a massive privacy and free speech nightmare.”
Utah became the first to adopt laws regulating children’s access to social media, followed by others, including Arkansas, Louisiana, Ohio, Texas, Florida and New York, though approaches have varied.
Countries around the world have also moved to curb children’s access to harmful internet content, including a ban in Australia on social media for children under 16.

California’s version, known as Assembly Bill 1709, prohibits children under age 16 from exposure to a number of “psychologically exploitative features intended to maximize engagement that foreseeably lead to compulsive use.”
Those include infinite-scroll feeds, algorithmic autoplay and other features to be defined in future regulations.
Its enactment comes at a time when Big Tech, in the face of mounting legal challenges, has shown greater willingness to accept new restrictions.

Meta agreed three weeks ago to pay as much as $18 billion over the next decade and strictly limit how teenagers use its Facebook and Instagram platforms under a deal with nearly all US states to resolve civil claims that the company designed its social media platforms to addict children. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Pressure grows on Burnham to commit to increasing statutory paternity leave
articles.summary:
Exclusive: Calls from Labour grow as 105 MPs write to PM urging ‘obvious’ step to alleviate cost of living crisis

Andy Burnham is coming under increasing pressure from his own MPs to commit…

blocks.text: Andy Burnham is coming under increasing pressure from his own MPs to commit to improving paternity leave in the UK in the next budget, with more than a quarter of Labour MPs writing to the prime minister to urge him to take action.

Ahead of the chancellor’s first budget next month, 105 MPs have written to Burnham calling on him to increase statutory paternity leave to help alleviate the cost of living crisis and arguing that lowest-paid fathers are the hardest hit by meagre paternity leave provision.

Momentum is growing on the Labour benches for action to be taken on parental leave, with many arguing it is a headline-grabbing policy that they say would cut through with voters. MPs have their sights set on the government’s parental leave review, which is due in December, but many are hoping Burnham could take definitive action before then.

The Guardian understands that almost half of Labour’s 403 MPs have explicitly supported improvement to paternity leave, including two secretaries of state, 11 ministers, six whips and nearly two dozen parliamentary private secretaries. “That’s nearly a quarter of all government office holders, and plenty more have indicated support in private,” said one supporter.

In the letter to Burnham from MPs, seen by the Guardian, parliamentarians urge the prime minister to take the “obvious” step of increasing paid paternity leave to tackle the cost of living crisis. They point out that in his constituency of Makerfield half of all fathers will not be able to afford to take paternity leave.

Coordinated by the influential Labour peer and former Trades Union Congress (TUC) general secretary Frances O’Grady and the MPs Maya Ellis and Jon Pearce, the letter calls on Burnham and the chancellor, John Healey, to help families with babies, who they say are at the “sharp end of the cost of living crisis”.

Noting that, according to HMRC data, more leave is taken in south-east England and London than in Scotland, Wales, Northern Ireland and north-west and north-east England combined, and that 90% of the paternity leave that is claimed goes to higher earners, the letter argues that giving fathers six weeks’ leave paid at 90% of earnings would result in £2.6bn in economic growth. It adds that it would be “good growth, which sorting out the above geographic disparities would deliver into every postcode”.

O’Grady said there was a growing consensus in the Labour ranks that the eye-catching policy would be welcomed by voters, particularly among blue-collar workers, who were the most likely to miss out on paternity leave.

“I think the moment has come, because I do think Andy Burnham has shown that he gets the pressures of everyday life,” she said. “He promised hope in every heart and I can’t think of a better way of building that optimism in our future than giving a better start to babies. This could genuinely transform everyday lives, and it’s something that people would cherish for ever.”
after newsletter promotion

Campaigners have long argued that the UK has one of the least generous paternity offers in the world, with the UK ranked 40th out of 43 OECD countries. Employed fathers in the UK get two weeks’ statutory paternity leave paid at £187.18 a week (less than half the “national living wage”), which accounts for only 1.9% of all government spending on parental leave.

At the start of the month, 48 charities, unions and academics called on Burnham to overhaul parental leave to make having a family more financially viable. The group – which included the Fawcett Society, Movember, the TUC and Mumsnet – warned that the current system resulted in “stark” consequences, with a report last year by Maternity Action finding that 55% of women on maternity leave said they borrowed money to cover their living costs.

“This is not just a question of how we support families in the first year of a child’s life,” they wrote. “It is about what kind of society and economy we want to build; financial pressures make parenthood less attractive and less feasible, with significant implications for the economy and society.”

In August, thousands of parents took part in a “parent strike” organised by the campaign groups Mother Pukka and the Dad Shift to call for better parental leave, with demonstrations in London, Edinburgh, Glasgow, Brighton and Oxford.

George Gabriel, a co-founder of the Dad Shift, said: “With working families expecting a newborn among the most exposed to the price shocks and proof in country after country that improving paternity leave boosts women’s economic prospects, this is one of a tiny handful of policies that is both a measure to drive good growth in every postcode and to tackle the cost of living.”

A government spokesperson said it was determined to make sure that dads and partners can be there to provide support to their families after childbirth. “Changes we’ve already made brought an additional 32,000 partners into scope for paternity leave and we are carrying out a full review of parental pay and leave to ensure we reflect the realities of modern work and childcare.”

articles.title: Remembrance ceremonies to be held across the US to honor victims of 9/11
articles.summary:
Memorials and remembrances will mark the 25 years since the attacks that killed nearly 3,000 on 11 September 2001

The United States is marking the 25th

blocks.text: The United States is marking the 25th anniversary of the 11 September 2001 terrorist attacks on Friday, with memorials and remembrance ceremonies taking place across the country to honor the nearly 3,000 people killed in the attacks.

In New York City, the national September 11 memorial and museum will hold its annual commemoration ceremony, with the families of victims gathering at the 9/11 Memorial Plaza and reading aloud the names of those killed in the 9/11 attacks and in the 1993 World Trade Center bombing.

The 25th commemoration ceremony will begin at 8:30am local time. Seven moments of silence will be observed throughout the ceremony, marking the times when each of the towers was struck and fell, as well as the times of the attack on the Pentagon in Arlington county, Virginia, and the crash of Flight 93 in Pennsylvania, “and to honor those who lost their lives to 9/11-related illness and injury in the years since”, according to the museum.
Current and former New York City leaders and other political figures are also expected to attend the ceremony, including the city’s mayor, Zohran Mamdani.

The New York Times reported this month that former president Joe Biden and former first lady Jill Biden, as well as former presidents Barack Obama, George W Bush and Bill Clinton, and former secretary of state Hillary Clinton, are also expected to attend.
Donald Trump is expected to commemorate the anniversary at the Pentagon, where American Airlines Flight 77 crashed after being hijacked. JD Vance is expected to attend the New York ceremony.

On Wednesday night in New York City, a drone show featuring 2,977 lights, one for each person killed in the attacks, illuminated the skies over New York Harbor, before forming the outline of the twin towers.

Friday’s memorial ceremonies come just days after the Mamdani administration released more than 170,000 documents related to the health concerns, air quality and city’s response to the attacks, including records suggesting that New Yorkers were misled about the safety of the air quality after the attacks.

Also on Friday morning, New York City firefighters are scheduled to hold a ceremony at the FDNY firefighters memorial on Manhattan’s Upper West Side to honor the 343 members of the department who lost their lives on September 11.

In Virginia, the national 9/11 Pentagon memorial will be closed to the public from 3am through noon on Friday for the Pentagon’s 25th anniversary 9/11 observance ceremony, with the exception of any victim’s families, survivors or survivor’s families.

In Pennsylvania, a ceremony is also planned at the Flight 93 national memorial, where United Airlines Flight 93 crashed after being hijacked. The morning observance will include a reading of the names of the passengers and crew members, followed by the ringing of the bells of remembrance. The afternoon ceremony is set to feature “remarks, keynote speakers, music and concludes with a public wreath-laying ceremony at the Wall of Names”, according to the National Park Service.

On Saturday, another ceremony will take place at the Flight 93 national memorial, where 40 candle lanterns will be carried to the Wall of Names and placed beneath the names of each passenger and crew member.
Additional ceremonies and memorial events are scheduled on Friday across the country as communities mark 25 years since the attacks.

articles.title: Why isn't Canada blocking the Welland Canal? Other trade war questions answered
articles.summary: CBC News readers, viewers and listeners have been sending in questions about the trade war, often asking how Canada can turn up the heat on the U.S.

image.caption: Boats sit idle in Lake Ontario close to the Welland Canal on Oct. 26, 2023. (Tara Walton/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Canada·New
CBC News readers, viewers and listeners have been sending in questions about the trade war, often asking how Canada can turn up the heat on the U.S.
CBC News answers your questions about export taxes, sales bans and toilet paper
Can Canada actually win a trade war with the U.S.? | About That

Reading through the emails that readers send to CBC News, one gets the impression they don't want just "elbows up" in the Canada-U.S. trade war, but also sticks, knees, skates and whatever else might be lying around.
One of the most common questions is some variation of, "Why isn't Canada doing X?" — where X is a tactic or tariff the reader supposes will hit the U.S. where it hurts.
Here's a look at some of those suggestions and what key players or observers have had to say about them.
Why doesn't Canada put export duties on energy as the cost is borne by Americans not Canadians?

Don Drummond, former chief economist for TD Bank, told CBC News late last month that export taxes are an option. Former prime minister Jean Chrétien said this week that an export tax on oil, gas, electricity and potash might be needed.
In 2025, Canadian commodities accounted for 63 per cent of oil imported into the U.S., 81 per cent of imported electricity, 99 per cent of imported natural gas and 80 per cent of imported potash.

However, Wolfgang Alschner, the Hyman Soloway Chair in Business and Trade Law at the University of Ottawa, warned that the long-term effects of such a move could be severe for Canada, both through lost revenue and damage to the relationship with its biggest customer. The U.S. could respond much as Canada has to U.S. President Donald Trump's tariffs: by trying to diversify away from a partner it can no longer count on and finding new suppliers.

items: Canada has leverage in this trade fight, but economists warn it comes with a cost
The art of inflicting pain: How to select targets for Canada's counter-tariffs

blocks.text: University of Calgary economist Trevor Tombe and Christopher Ragan, founding director of McGill University's Max Bell School of Public Policy, made the same point separately: targeting U.S. energy could play into the hands of the U.S. administration and unite Americans against Canada.
Prime Minister Mark Carney said in July he doesn't "see the value" in using energy exports as a bargaining chip. Carney said being a reliable supplier is important.
"Canadians are reliable. Canadians can be trusted," he said.
Why not ban sales of certain goods in Canada?
This has mostly already happened at a provincial level with alcohol, in every province except Alberta and Saskatchewan. Saskatchewan this week added a retaliatory levy on U.S. alcohol.
Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne has shown no interest in that sort of approach, stressing that Canada's response will be proportionate, strategic and targeted.

items: Poilievre tells U.S. TV Canadians are 'wounded' and 'confused' to be in America's crosshairs
Trade war, Alberta referendum loom large as Carney charts cabinet's year forward

blocks.text: The U.S. may, of course, reply in kind to any ban, as it has with alcohol: Most imports of Canadian-made alcohol will be banned from the United States on Sept. 29.

Tombe, discussing tariffs, told CBC News late last month that Canada has to be careful when selecting products to target because they need to be items Canadians can replace relatively easily but Americans cannot.

If tariffs are applied to harder-to-replace items — "a particular type of circuit board, say, or piece of machinery," that merely complicates life and increases costs for the Canadian importer, Tombe said.
Is toilet paper an unlikely pressure point in the Canada–U.S. trade war?
Can Canada stop U.S. ships using the Welland Canal?

The Welland Canal is on the western half of the St. Lawrence Seaway, which connects the St. Lawrence River to the Great Lakes. The canal links Lake Ontario to Lake Erie using eight locks, all in Ontario, that can be filled with water or drained to move vessels between different water levels.
But the seaway is overseen by both the U.S. and Canada.
The Great Lakes St. Lawrence Seaway Development Corporation administers the seaway on the American side as a federal agency within the U.S. Department of Transportation.
In Canada, the federal government owns the Canadian portion of the seaway, but it is managed by the non-profit St. Lawrence Seaway Management Corporation.
The U.S. also controls several important locks, including ones in New York state between Lake Ontario and Montreal and others in Michigan that connect Lake Superior and Lake Huron.

John Boscariol, a Toronto-based co-head of international trade and investment law at the Canadian law firm McCarthy Tétrault, told CHCH News in Hamilton that closing the canal would be "shooting ourselves in the foot" and would hurt Canadian businesses just as much as U.S. businesses.

Trump critic Jennifer Hillman, formerly general counsel at the Office of the United States Trade Representative under then-president Bill Clinton, told CBC News Network it would "absolutely be a total violation of international law, and I think not really a good idea because you're blocking both sides' goods.
"I would hope that's not a road anybody would go down."
What questions do you have about the latest tariffs? Send an email to ask@cbc.ca.
With files from CBC's Peter Zimonjic, Darren Major and Evan Dyer and The Canadian Press

articles.title: Wildfires, permafrost melt in Canada causing even more climate change, new study shows
articles.summary: These climate feedback loops, where climate change triggers more greenhouse gas emissions that in turn feed into even more climate change, could add 20 to 30 per cent more warming over current…

image.caption: A wildfire near Okanagan Lake in B.C. in August. Growing wildfire emissions along with other emissions induced by climate change are feeding into even more global warming. (Darryl Dyck/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Science·New

These climate feedback loops, where climate change triggers more greenhouse gas emissions that in turn feed into even more climate change, could add 20 to 30 per cent more warming over current estimates for this century.
New research says current climate models don’t account for warming-induced emissions
We know that global warming has made wildfires worse, and melted permafrost that's been frozen for years.

Now, a new study is detailing how the fires, permafrost thaw and other changes are adding even more greenhouse gases into the atmosphere, and speeding up climate change at a scale not currently reflected in global estimates.

These climate "feedback loops," where climate change triggers more carbon emissions that in turn feed into even more climate change, could add 20 to 30 per cent more warming over current estimates for this century, according to a new study by researchers at U.S. institutions, including Stanford University and the non-profits Environmental Defense Fund and Spark Climate Solutions.
"Our remaining carbon budget is most likely ... much smaller than what we think it is," said Ben Poulter, program director with Spark Climate Solutions and co-author of the paper.
“If you don't include these additional feedbacks, we're going to have a disconnect between the policy targets and how the Earth system is responding to climate change.”

The paper, published on Thursday in the journal Environmental Research Letters, is one of the most comprehensive reviews to date of these warming-induced emissions and their impact on global temperature rise. Current climate models mostly track emissions from anthropogenic sources — the burning of fossil fuels for energy, food production and cattle rearing, decomposing waste and other human activities that release greenhouse gases.
The findings have particular significance for Canada, which is home to a large chunk of these warming-induced emissions.
Happening here
As a northern country, Canada is already warming faster than the rest of the world.

This September, the federal government released its landmark Canada’s Changing Climate assessment, which said that the country could be heading to a whopping five degrees of warming in this century, bringing with it profound changes to people, ecosystems and landscapes.

items: Canadians should prepare for a 5 C hotter future, report warns
Wildfires send Canada's carbon emissions soaring. And our peatlands emit even more
University of Alberta researchers looking to quantify climate change impact of carbon released from permafrost

blocks.text: The new paper brings into view how the changes in Canada won’t just be felt locally, but feed into climate change globally. It draws on previous research already highlighting the impacts of specific extreme weather events.

For example, during Canada's worst wildfire season on record in 2023, the flames released one billion tonnes of carbon. If they were a country, the wildfires would have been the eighth highest emitter in the world.

“Canada is a large northern country, so these feedbacks is going to occur within Canada to a large degree,” said David Olefeldt, professor at the University of Alberta and a leading permafrost researcher.
“Therefore we have a responsibility to make sure we have studies that are focusing on it.”
Why is the permafrost melting?

Rising temperatures from global warming are heating up the Arctic at two or three times the global average, and that’s leading to the permafrost thawing. But while previously permafrost thaw was seen as a gradual process happening throughout the region, Poulter said the new paper included emissions from the process of "abrupt" thawing.

The abrupt thawing, also triggered by warming as well as extreme weather like wildfires and rain, happens much more locally and causes the land to cave or slump suddenly. Olefeldt said that while these abrupt thaws happen over smaller areas, usually at the edges of wetlands and lakes, they have the potential to release much more carbon.
The abrupt thaw exposes the soil, and the ancient organic material that was previously locked up in it, to microbes that feed on that soil and produce methane and carbon dioxide.
“You're creating new lakes or new wetlands, for example, or warming the soil quite a lot faster in those locations,” he said.
But coming up with exact estimates of how much carbon is being released is tough.

“We have very sparse measurement networks in the high latitudes just because of the remoteness of the sites, the challenges for doing research in these areas,” Poulter said, pointing to a need, especially in Canada, for more field studies to monitor this process.
The wetland methane puzzle
Another major source of warming-induced emissions are wetlands, which cover large parts of Canada.

Scientists have grown increasingly worried about methane emissions from wetlands because of a major spike in the growth of methane in the atmosphere starting around 2020, Poulter said. The emissions growth could not be fully explained by direct human activities like oil and gas production and agriculture, which produce methane, and attention turned toward wetlands.
Lisa Stein, a professor and microbiologist at the University of Alberta, said she hopes the new paper will push institutions to include freshwater wetlands in their climate models.

When microbes break down organic matter in wetlands, methane is created as a byproduct of that biological process and emitted into the atmosphere. Warmer temperatures increase that microbial metabolism and therefore create more methane, Stein said.

“When scientists have looked at methane increase in the atmosphere over the last five years, they've noted that almost all of it has the signature of biology,” Stein said, meaning that rising methane emissions can't fully be explained by human activities and are also being driven by this rise in microbial activity.
Warmer winters, where lakes don't freeze as long, matter too, Poulter said.
“As we see the frozen season get shorter and shorter, we're seeing sort of an increasing duration of these persistent methane emissions coming out of Canada's wetlands,” he said.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Inayat Singh covers the environment and climate change at CBC News. He is based in Toronto and has previously reported from Winnipeg. Email: inayat.singh@cbc.ca

articles.title: Canadian teens score well on OECD tests, but sharp drops in reading, math raise concerns
articles.summary: Canadian teens have strong knowledge of science, reading and math, according to a major international assessment, but the OECD's latest PISA results also indicate a long-term slide in test scores for…

image.caption: Canadian teens have good knowledge of science, reading and math, according to a major international assessment, but the latest PISA results also show a long-term slide in all three subjects, with a steep and worrisome drop more recently in the latter two. (Evan Mistui/CBC)

blocks.text: Canadian teens have good knowledge of science, reading and math, according to a major international assessment, but the latest PISA results also indicate a long-term slide in scores for all three subjects, with a steep and worrisome drop in the latter two over the past few editions.

That downward trend — amid an overall decline for teens worldwide — raises concerns for some educators and researchers, who hope the latest results propel policymakers toward more consideration and action to improve student learning.

The joint body comprising all Canadian ministers of education and higher education noted as much in a statement earlier this week, saying, "comparative results over time emphasize the imperative for ongoing attention to educational outcomes."

Held every three years, the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)'s Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) tests 15-year-olds in about 90 countries and economies worldwide on three subjects, with a heavier, rotating focus on one subject each edition.

For the 2025 edition, about 24,600 students across Canada participated (Yukon, Northwest Territories and Nunavut did not participate and are not represented in the results). Additional data about student attitudes, behaviours and school atmosphere was gathered from student and school principal questionnaires.
Experts blame AI, screens for slipping Canadian student test scores
The latest results show Canadian students rank above the OECD average and among the upper tier of top-performing PISA participants globally.
Canadian students scored 510 points in science, 490 in reading and 485 in math. Students from China and Singapore were the highest performers.

Yet comparing Canadians' performance to past editions shows a notable decline over two decades. Canada has slipped gradually in science (24 points since 2006) and fallen sharply in reading and math (declining 37 and 42 points respectively since 2006, with a drop of 30 and 27 points alone since 2018).
Though small variations in scores are expected, the OECD considers changes greater than 20 points (which represent a school year's worth of learning) statistically significant.
"If a country’s score falls by 20 points between two PISA assessments, it is as if students were performing at the level expected of 14-year-olds in the previous cycle," it says.

"The steepness of these declines post-pandemic is ... what some would call shocking. I would call it very concerning," said Louis Volante, a professor at Brock University who researches international achievement testing, educational governance and policy.

Volante points to factors that researchers think are impacting student achievement: more digital distractions, increased use of artificial intelligence since the last edition and teacher shortages worldwide.
"When you put those three together, they are being attributed to really having a negative impact on overall rating scores," he said from Oakville, Ont.

The 2025 edition had the lowest OECD-average performance observed so far, the organization said. After an unprecedented drop in performance in 2022 — the first edition reflecting the disruptions of COVID-19 — learning outcomes across all participants stagnated or continued to fall in 2025, OECD Secretary-General Mathias Cormann wrote in a report detailing the latest results.

items: Parents are pushing back on classroom screen time in a 'techlash' over too much technology in schools
In the age of AI, how do we teach young people to think critically?

blocks.text: He singled out an overall steep drop in reading scores as particularly of note "because reading skills underpin learning across the curriculum and are essential for finding, evaluating, interpreting and reflecting on information in an increasingly digital world."
Countries with the largest reading declines also tended to see the largest drops in science and math, he said.

It's something seen in classrooms, as well. Both with her students in the West Quebec School Board and the University of Ottawa, Tasha Ausman has noticed a decline in student reading comprehension and ability to identify key information.
During a test for an advanced math class this week, "students were asking me things that were directly written in the question," the high school teacher and university educator shared as an example.
Meanwhile, her post-secondary students regularly email questions easily answered at the start of her syllabus — like which textbook to buy or where to buy it.

items: Is the age of reading over?

blocks.text: She praises students today as empathetic as they team up with classmates, eager to learn and connect and excited by hands-on learning. Yet she's also found them much more stressed by tests and struggling with some basics.
"It's not a lack of willingness. I think it's an actual literacy challenge."
Canada slow to change, says consultant

In the past, Canada was a top 10 PISA participant, but our school systems have since weakened and we've been slow to respond, says education consultant Paul Bennett, director of Schoolhouse Institute.

The PISA results are "a cause for alarm, especially given the dramatic declines since 2015. The trends that were visible in 2022 after the pandemic are proving to be more permanent than we ever imagined," he said from Halifax.
"We've lost ground to the countries in Asia who have focused much more on test preparation. They're much more in favour of direct instruction. They've had great success in teaching that way."

Given that education is a provincial rather than federal responsibility in Canada, as well as the different socioeconomic and other challenges in each jurisdiction, Bennett feels Canada has been inconsistent with education policy updates and changes.

He noted, for instance, that in provinces with higher PISA scores — Alberta, Ontario, British Columbia and Quebec — "there's much more of a focus on the science of learning," he noted. "They were early onto it. They've begun to match their teaching methodologies with what works in the classroom."
Bennett thinks a host of practices require fresh consideration, from screen learning and technology use to a comeback for physical textbooks.
"I don't want to turn back the clock," he said, "but we need to readjust our focus."
An indicator for the future
What's behind sliding student performance is a billion-dollar question for everyone, says Darryl Hunter, a recently retired education professor at the University of Alberta.

PISA, national tests like the Pan-Canadian Assessment Program and provincial assessments are designed to serve as periodic status checks, Hunter explained — to inspire deeper conversation, thorough investigation and new research to guide educational policymakers.
"If Canada is going to be a dynamic country in the future, we have to attend to the performance of our students."
While PISA results are a high-profile measure, Volante at Brock University cautions it should be taken in perspective and that comparing test scores shouldn't be the sole focus.

The student and principal questionnaires dive into what Volante called "non-cognitive" aspects, things like whether students are curious, seek help or believe in their own ability to achieve, as well as school attendance, if they read for pleasure, feel they belong and whether they receive family support.
Those indicators contribute to a more holistic picture of how schools are doing, he said, noting that faring well in these areas is linked to stronger student outcomes.
"Success in the future will not solely be dictated by how well [students] do in reading, math and science," Volante said.

"We hear a lot of rhetoric around, 'We need our reading and math and our science scores to go up so that we can improve our economy.' But I would argue 'Yes, we do, but we also need all these other things as well.'"

articles.title: Man loses case to claw back $369,000 he spent on lavish gifts for ex-girlfriend
articles.summary: Singapore's High Court rules in the woman's favour, with the judge saying the man "willingly" showered her with gifts, even before they got together.

blocks.text: A Singaporean man has lost a court case to claw back hundreds of thousands of dollars that he had lavished on his ex-girlfriend while they were together.
The S$468,000 ($369,200; £273,260) that Chander Agarwal attempted to recover from Felicia Lee was money he had "willingly" spent on her, the Singapore High Court ruled.
Agarwal "displayed a consistent pattern of showering [Lee] with lavish gifts" even before they got together and would reassure her that he did not expect repayment, Senior Judge Lee Seiu Kin said.

Agarwal, the CEO of a logistics company, met Felicia Lee, a former flight attendant, during a flight in 2019. They were in a romantic relationship from September 2022 to December 2023, the court heard.
Their relationship fell apart after Agarwal suspected Lee of having an affair.
Agarwal, who launched the suit in March 2024, argued that Lee had "requested various interest-free loans" from him over the course of their relationship.

He claimed that these included S$206,000 in credit card charges, S$129,000 for overseas trips, S$17,000 to engage a fengshui master for her apartment, and S$20,000 to pay for her life insurance premiums.
Lee argued that these were "gifts made out of love and affection" and not loans.

In agreeing with Lee, the judge noted that Agarwal's case lacked documentary evidence - for instance, he could not produce any proof that Lee had acknowledged receipt of the loans that she had allegedly requested.
"The evidence before me clearly shows that the claimant, smitten by the defendant, had showered her with expensive gifts during their relationship," the judge said.
"Unfortunately, when their relationship ended on a sour note, [Agarwal] became embittered and was determined to extract a price from her."
The judge also noted that Agarwal was "clearly a man of ample means who has expensive tastes", in contrast to Lee "who was not in that league".
In many text messages Lee had "expressed her awe when [Agarwal] suggested expensive gifts, and on occasion, her spontaneous reluctance to accept them", the judge noted.

In concluding his written judgement, the judge cited English playwright William Congreve, who wrote in his tragedy satire The Mourning Bride: "Heav'n has no rage, like love to hatred turn'd, nor hell a fury, like a woman scorn'd."
"This case shows that such emotion is not the sole province of one gender," he said.
In early 2023, another Singaporean man had filed two lawsuits – in claims amounting to over S$3m - against a woman who rejected his romantic advances.
K Kawshigan claimed that Nora Tan's rejection brought him emotional trauma and caused damage to his reputation.
The Singapore courts struck out his suits. Tan later counter-sued Kawshigan to claim back expenses she said she had incurred while defending herself from his alleged harassment.

articles.title: Romualdez to be moved from Cardinal Santos to PGH
articles.summary: Court seeks independent medical review before ruling on his confinement.

blocks.text: September 11, 2026 | 3:57pm

Rep. Martin Romualdez (Leyte) lies in a hospital bed at Cardinal Santos Medical Center as police place him under custody on Sept. 7, 2026, following the Sandiganbayan's issuance of a warrant in a P7.44-billion plunder case.
Philstar.com / Contributed photo

MANILA, Philippines — Former House speaker Martin Romualdez will be transferred to the Philippine General Hospital on Saturday, September 12, for an independent medical assessment as the Sandiganbayan weighs his request to remain under hospital confinement.

The Sandiganbayan Third Division announced the transfer Friday during the continuation of hearings on Romualdez's motion to remain at Cardinal Santos Medical Center in San Juan City, The STAR reported.
Romualdez is set to remain at PGH until further order from the court.

The transfer would place Romualdez in a government hospital while giving the court an independent assessment of the medical conditions his lawyers have cited to justify his continued confinement outside a regular detention facility.

Romualdez's camp earlier asked the Sandiganbayan to allow him to remain at Cardinal Santos, citing cardiovascular conditions, Type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, dyslipidemia and primary hypothyroidism.

The Office of the Ombudsman and the Department of the Interior and Local Government opposed his continued confinement at the private hospital and sought his transfer to the Philippine National Police General Hospital at Camp Crame.
Hearings on Romualdez's motion began Thursday. He did not appear in court after his doctors certified that he was "unfit to travel."

The Sandiganbayan also issued a commitment order Thursday placing Romualdez under the custody of the Bureau of Jail Management and Penology and committing him to the New Quezon City Jail Male Dormitory as a detention prisoner.
The court, however, had not yet ordered his physical transfer to the jail as it continued hearing his request for hospital confinement.
Romualdez was arrested September 7 while confined at Cardinal Santos after the Sandiganbayan found probable cause and issued a warrant in a P7.44-billion plunder case.

Prosecutors accuse Romualdez and three others of receiving at least P7.44 billion in alleged kickbacks and other financial benefits from contractors and parties with interests in flood-control, infrastructure and other government projects from 2022 to 2025.
Romualdez has denied wrongdoing and said through his counsel that he would face the allegations in accordance with law.

blocks.text: Published September 11, 2026 3:54pm
The Supreme Court (SC) has dismissed the complaint filed by the Office of the Ombudsman against seven associate justices of the Court of Appeals (CA) for alleged gross ignorance of the law.
In a resolution dated December 2025, the SC dismissed the administrative complaint against the justices for being judicial in nature and lacking of merit.
The respondents were Associate Justices Marlene Gonzales-Sison, Rafael Antonio Santos, Louis Acosta, Roberto Quiroz, Rex Bernardo Pascual, Mary Charlene Hernandez-Azura, and Ferdinand Baylon.
The complaint stemmed from the justices' issuance of a temporary restraining order (TRO) against a preventive suspension order involving eight members of the Sangguniang Panlalawigan of Antique.
Last week, Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla urged the SC to act on the complaint, which was filed by his predecessor, Samuel Martires. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: MPs to vote again on assisted dying as bill returns to parliament – UK politics live
articles.summary:
Bill would allow terminally ill adults with less than six months to live to end their lives, after the approval of a panel of experts

Morning, and welcome to our UK politics blog.…

blocks.text: Assisted dying bill returns to the Commons

Morning, and welcome to our UK politics blog. The assisted dying bill is back in the Commons today, where MPs will vote on a proposal that would allow adults in England and Wales with less than six months to live to seek medical assistance to end their lives.

MPs had previously voted through the Terminally Ill Adults (End of Life) Bill, brought forward by Labour MP Kim Leadbeater, in June 2025, but it foundered in the House of Lords earlier this year after opponents tabled more than 1,280 amendments. Prime minister Andy Burnham has confirmed he will not vote, saying he does not want to “unduly influence the debate”.

blocks.caption: Supporters of assisted dying demonstrate outside parliament in April 2026. Photograph: Wiktor Szymanowicz/Future Publishing/Getty Images

blocks.text: The bill has been revived by Labour MP Lauren Edwards, who said there was “a real human cost to the delay in passing this legislation and correcting the injustices and cruelty of the current law”. Two Labour MPs have also warned of “extraordinary risks” if ministers try to force the assisted dying bill using an obscure parliamentary procedure, should it continue to be blocked by the Lords. My colleagues Jessica Elgot and Peter Walker have the full report here:

If the bill is voted through, it will then go through further debate and possible amendments before MPs vote on it again at third reading. It would then move to the Lords for scrutiny before returning to the Commons.
If the bill passes, the UK would join European countries such as Austria, Belgium, the Netherlands, Spain and Switzerland, as well as Australia, Canada and the US, where it is legal in 13 states.
The Commons debate begins at 9.30am, with a vote scheduled for 2.30pm. We’ll bring you the latest developments throughout the day.
Key events

items: 9m agoEsther Rantzen now ‘too physically fragile’ to end her life in Switzerland
13m agoAssisted dying bill returns to the Commons

blocks.text: Esther Rantzen now ‘too physically fragile’ to end her life in Switzerland
Raphael Boyd
Esther Rantzen has said she is no longer able to travel to Switzerland to end her life because she has become “too physically fragile”.

Rantzen, who presented the TV current affairs programme That’s Life! for 21 years and founded the youth support charity Childline, had intended to end her life in a Dignitas assisted dying clinic in Switzerland after being diagnosed with terminal lung cancer in 2023.

blocks.caption: Esther Rantzen had intended to end her life in Swiss clinic after being diagnosed with terminal lung cancer in 2023. Photograph: Cheese Scientist/Alamy

blocks.text: The broadcaster, 86, said in a statement on Thursday that her quality of life had deteriorated since her diagnosis, and that she was ready to end her life but was no longer able to make the journey despite having joined Dignitas about a year after learning she was terminally ill.
Rantzen said: “Unfortunately, when I was strong enough to make the flight and go to Dignitas, my life was not unbearably painful, indeed, I was able to relax in my beloved cottage in the New Forest.
“And by the time life did become unbearable, I was too physically fragile to make the journey and go through the Dignitas process.
“So even though I had spent the money and made the plans, I was not ready to end my life back then, and did not realise that would be my last chance.”

articles.title: Firefighters enter charred ferry as search continues for dozens missing in Palawan
articles.summary: The Philippine Coast Guard revises the number of missing from 86 to 84 after authorities verified two people originally listed on the manifest had not been on board. The number of people rescued…

blocks.text: SEARCH AND RESCUE OPERATIONS. Authorities and responders board a vessel to assist ongoing search and rescue operations involving the MV June Aster ferry, which caught fire off the coast of Palawan, Philippines, September 11, 2026.
Eloisa Lopez/REUTERS

The Philippine Coast Guard revises the number of missing from 86 to 84 after authorities verified two people originally listed on the manifest had not been on board. The number of people rescued stood at 43.

items: A ferry fire in the Philippines on September 11 resulted in five deaths and over 80 missing, with 43 survivors rescued.
Firefighters faced challenges due to thick smoke and heat before boarding the ferry, which was carrying 117 passengers and 17 crew members.
The cause of the fire remains unclear, but survivor accounts mention two explosions prior to the blaze; the ferry was also carrying various vehicles and cargo.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – Frefighters on Friday, September 11, managed to board a burned-out ferry more than a day after the ship caught fire on its way from Manila to the western province of Palawan, killing five people and leaving more than 80 missing.

Thick smoke and extreme heat had prevented firefighters from boarding the ferry,which a manifest said was carrying 117 passengers and 17 crew members when it was engulfed in flames on Wednesday night.

The Philippine Coast Guard revised the number of missing from 86 to 84 after authorities verified two people originally listed on the manifest had not been on board. The number of people rescued stood at 43.

Aerial footage showed a Coast Guard helicopter hovering above the burned ferry, whose upper decks were blackened by fire. While light smoke continued to rise from parts of the vessel, it was noticeably thinner than the thick plumes seen a day earlier. Two firefighters could be seen on an upper deck.

Richard Marceliano, one of the survivors, told GMA News he saw a small amount of smoke that quickly turned into a raging fire and spread through the ferry within seconds. He said he and other passengers spent nearly two hours floating in the sea before they were rescued.

Outside the office of shipowner Atienza Inter-Island Ferries in Manila, frustrated relatives of missing passengers waited for information about their loved ones after failing to get updates from the company by phone.

Evelyn Umpad, 64, said she went to the shipowner’s office after the company failed to answer her repeated calls seeking information about her son and daughter-in-law, who were travelling to the town of Taytay in Palawan to buy land.

“We kept calling but nobody was answering. They took my number and said they would call back, but no one contacted us, so we came here ourselves to find out the situation,” Umpad said. “My appeal is for them to take action and keep us updated.”
The ferry company has said it was fully cooperating with government authorities investigating the incident.

The Coast Guard has deployed five vessels and divers to the area, while army rescue boats, fishermen and private resort owners continued to assist in the search that began on Wednesday night. Coast Guard spokesperson Commodore Noemie Cayabyab said the Coast Guard would also deploy a larger vessel.

It remained unclear what started the blaze, which broke out as the ferry neared the end of its more than 20-hour voyage to Coron, a popular tourist spot in northern Palawan. A statement from the Maritime Industry Authority (MARINA), citing survivor accounts, said two successive explosions were heard from within the ship, which triggered the fire.
The ferry, with capacity for 330 people, was also carrying five motorcycles, an electric vehicle, a forklift, a pickup truck and mostly cargo goods, according to the Coast Guard.
Ferry travel is a common mode of transport in the Philippines, an archipelago of more than 7,600 islands, where millions of people rely on boats to travel between provinces.
The country has a patchy maritime safety record, and many previous ferry disasters have been linked to overcrowding, rough weather and lax enforcement of safety regulations. – Rappler.com

MANILA, Philippines – The anti-graft court Sandiganbayan‘s 3rd Division ordered the transfer of Leyte 1st District Representative Martin Romualdez to the University of the Philippines-Philippine General Hospital (UP-PGH) for an independent medical examination on Saturday, September 12.
This means Romualdez would be discharged from the Cardinal Santos Medical Center in San Juan City on Saturday and then stay at UP-PGH in Manila until further orders from the anti-graft court.

Sandiganbayan Associate Justice Karl Miranda, the court division chairman, issued the order on Friday, September 11, during the second day of the court’s hearing for the lawmaker’s motion on Romualdez’s continued hospital confinement.

The former House speaker remained in hospital confinement at the Cardinal Santos Medical Center following his arrest on Monday, September 7, over his P7.44-billion plunder case in relation to the flood control mess.

blocks.caption: How Martin Romualdez avoided jail by going to hospital

blocks.text: The Bureau of Jail Management and Penology, the Philippine National Police, and the Office of the Judiciary Marshals would coordinate with the UP-PGH in bringing Romualdez to the hospital via an ambulance with the required medical equipment, according to the court order.

Romualdez’s doctors testified on the witness stand on Friday to explain his cardiological, neurological, and psychiatric conditions. All of them told the anti-graft court that transferring the lawmaker would be risky at the moment given the stress that he was experiencing.
UP-PGH doctors were directed to submit their report and recommendation on Sunday, September 13, and appear before the court on Monday, September 14.
Romualdez’s arraignment and pre-trial were reset to Wednesday, September 16. – Rappler.com

articles.title: ‘Amici curiae’: Where do invited ex-justices stand on conviction threshold debate?
articles.summary: Their past statements offer a glimpse into how they will guide the impeachment court

blocks.text: The Senate has tapped four former Supreme Court justices to be “amici curiae” or friends of the court in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte.

The four legal luminaries will advise senator-judges amid the ongoing debate on the minimum number needed to convict Duterte — a punishment that will remove her from office and could disqualify her from the 2028 presidential race.
Their past statements offer a glimpse into how they will guide the impeachment court.

blocks.caption: ‘Amici curiae’: Where do invited ex-justices stand on conviction threshold debate?

blocks.text: Azcuna, in an interview with ANC in June, argued that the conviction threshold should remain at 16 regardless of whether or not some senator-judges are detained or suspended.

At the time, Senator Bato dela Rosa was already in hiding, while Jinggoy Estrada was already in jail over plunder. As of writing, Senator Rodante Marcoleta has also been arrested for plunder, while Senator Loren Legarda has left the country due to medical reasons.

“My view is that the voting threshold is based on the number of members of the Senate, whether or not those members are present, or are present or able to actively participate, as long as they remain members of the Senate, they should be counted in computing the two-thirds,” Azcuna said.
He noted an exception though, believing the threshold could be reduced to 15 if Dela Rosa is considered to no longer be a senator because of his situation.

“If he is judged a fugitive, he can be considered, in my view, as resigned — constructive resignation. Being a fugitive entails running away from the legal system. If one runs away from the legal system, he relinquishes all membership in that system,” Azcuna explained.
Panganiban, in his Inquirer column, said that he believes Escudero’s 16-vote threshold ruling on the first day of the trial in July is “not set in stone.”

“He could reverse himself at any time, or the impeachment court can reverse or modify his ruling at the proper time. I believe that such ruling is merely interlocutory and does not become final until the decision is reached. Moreover, its reversal or modification requires only a simple majority, not two-thirds,” he wrote.

While he did not explicitly state what he believes is the magic number to secure a conviction, he raises the need to identify the “correct mathematical denominator.” As it stands, the denominator, as per Escudero’s ruling, is 24.

Panganiban cites the Supreme Court as an example, saying it “does not always compute its majority from its full complement of 15 members.” Its internal rules only require a quorum of at least eight members, and any decision can be made through the concurrence of a majority of members who take part in the deliberations.

“Consequently, the computation of the mathematical denominator shifts depending on active participation,” he said. Panganiban cites numerous rulings related to this: League of Cities v. Comelec in 2009, Cruz v. DENR Secretary in 2000, and De Castro v. Judicial and Bar Council in 2010.

Panganiban, however, clarified that such examples are “not for the Senate to follow blindly the Court’s method of ascertaining the voting denominator” because it “reviews only questions of law on facts proven in the trial courts, or admitted as true by the parties.”

blocks.caption: The case for 15: Does convicting Sara Duterte really need 16 votes?

blocks.text: Davide, who presided over the trial of former president Joseph Estrada, has not made any comment on the conviction threshold issue in Duterte’s trial, but his March 2018 interview on GMA News about scenarios on what was then a potential trial against then-chief justice Lourdes Sereno has resurfaced online.
At the time, the Senate had only 23 members, following the resignation of Alan Peter Cayetano to become Rodrigo Duterte’s foreign affairs chief.
His position was that the threshold remained at 16 despite the Senate being down one member.

“The only problem in the Senate is…two-thirds would be required to convict. So in this particular case, two-thirds, it will be 24, not existing 23. The Senate will need 16 to convict. In other words, since there are now 23, the vote of seven would be enough for acquittal,” Davide had said.
It remains to be seen whether he will adopt the same position today.

Puno has also not made a public comment on the conviction threshold debate, but as chairman of the Philippine Constitution Association, he criticized the Escudero-led Senate last year for returning the impeachment articles to the House of Representatives.

“Philconsa warns that it may constitute grave abuse of discretion and risks undermining the most fundamental principle of our constitutional democracy: that public office is a public trust,” Puno said.
Consultation with the amici curiae takes place on September 10. Davide will only submit a legal memo, while the three other former magistrates will appear in person. – Rappler.com

articles.title: New battery-powered trains will ‘bring faster journeys to north’
articles.summary:
No 10 says new fleet of trains built in Derby will support 6,000 jobs across UK

A new fleet of battery-powered trains will be built to “bring faster, more reliable journeys to the north”,…

blocks.text: A fleet of battery-powered trains is to be built to “bring faster, more reliable journeys to the north”, Downing Street has announced.

The 29 trains, which will be run by TransPennine Express, will be built at Alstom’s Litchurch Lane works in Derby from 2028, supporting 350 local jobs, and nearly 6,000 across the UK, according to the government.
The fleet will be made up of Adessia Stream trains, a battery-powered model that will be the first of its kind to be used for long-distance mainline journeys in the UK when it enters service in 2034.

Andy Burnham, who has repeatedly championed public transport and now travels between No 10 offices in London and Manchester, highlighted the need for more reliable and efficient services, with the new trains pitched as making journeys between major northern cities shorter while increasing capacity on rail networks by 30% in the next decade.
The trains will cut the journey time between Manchester and Leeds by up to 10 minutes, and between Manchester and York by up to 14 minutes.

The prime minister said: “I’ve lost count of the number of times someone has stopped me to tell me about the train that never came. And when that happens, it means missed shifts, missed appointments and missed opportunities.
“Today that starts to change. These 29 new trains will bring faster, more reliable journeys to the north, and thousands of British jobs for the next generation.
“It’s exactly what Great British Railways is all about – taking back control of the basics and getting Britain believing again.”
As well as speed and capacity, the new trains are set to run without emissions, even on non-electrified stretches of the network, while also having level-access boarding and onboard wifi.

The Transport secretary, Heidi Alexander, said the plans were a sign of how Great British Railways “will deliver better journeys for people while backing British business” and allowing passengers to “wave goodbye to overcrowded, delayed diesel trains and step onboard faster electric trains which are fit for the future”.

Alstom, the French train ⁠maker, said the contract was worth about €1.2bn (£1bn), including about €930m for the rolling stock and €230m in maintenance agreements. The latter will run for eight years, with the potential for a further eight-year extension.
after newsletter promotion
The company said the fleet of trains, which will be 121 metres long and run at speeds of up to 110mph, will be delivered from 2032.
Charging infrastructure will be installed in Hull, Scarborough and Saltburn – a UK-first on the mainline network – allowing the fleet to be recharged during normal operations.

“This agreement is a landmark moment for Britain’s railway,” said Rob Whyte, Alstom’s managing director in the UK. “The fleet will transform journeys across northern England while showcasing the very best of British engineering, innovation and advanced manufacturing.”
