articles.title: Iceland to submit bill that could ban whaling in its waters
articles.summary:
The country is one of just three that still permits commercial whaling, while its government has faced mounting pressure to ban the practice

Iceland will submit a bill in February 2027 which…

blocks.text: Iceland will submit a bill in February 2027 which could permanently ban whaling in its waters, a move that would leave Norway and Japan as the only two countries to permit commercial whaling.

Whaling in Iceland has been put under intense scrutiny since a government-commissioned report was published in 2023 that found harpooned whales took two hours to die. The report led to a temporary suspension of the hunt that year.

The bill, announced on the Icelandic government’s website, follows comments by Iceland’s minister of industries, Hanna Katrín Friðriksson, earlier this year calling for changes in the whaling laws she said were outdated and expressing support for an end to the whale hunt.
Wendy Higgins, of Humane World for Animals (HWA), an animal welfare group, said the bill was a “significant milestone” in efforts to end the practice.

“There is considerable political and public support for this bill to ban commercial whaling, and compelling ethical, veterinary, legal and conservation reasons to hope it succeeds,” said Higgins. “Every whale killed by exploding harpoon in Icelandic waters, is a tragic loss of life needlessly taken for an industry that has no purpose. A law to stop the killing can’t come soon enough.”

So far this year, up to 8 September, 80 fin whales were caught in Icelandic waters, according to HWA. The hunting season runs from June to the end of September and Iceland’s quota is up to 150 animals.

Fin whales are the second-largest animals on Earth, second to blue whales, and are classified as vulnerable to extinction by the International Union for Conservation of Nature, despite decades of recovery after the commercial whaling moratorium in 1986.
Iceland has only one remaining whaling company, Hvalur, run by Kristján Loftsson. A previous interim government in Iceland issued a five-year permit to Hvalur, which runs until 2029.

Higgins said: “Of course, campaigners want an immediate end to the killing of whales, but we also recognise that even if a ban is introduced, it’s likely that the current whaling permits, which expire in 2029, will be allowed to run their course.”

Sharon Livermore, the director of marine conservation at the International Fund for Animal Welfare (IFAW) said: “A proposal to update the laws that allow whaling in Icelandic waters would be a groundbreaking step towards modern day marine conservation and animal welfare, especially for a country so reliant on a healthy ocean.”

Just three countries – Iceland, Norway and Japan – have hunted for whales commercially in recent years. Norway resumed commercial whaling in 1993, and Iceland in 2006, despite a moratorium by the International Whaling Commission.
Japan left the IWC in 2019 and resumed commercial whaling in its waters.

articles.title: What Supreme Court's Imelda Marcos acquittal means, and what it doesn't
articles.summary: The Supreme Court has overturned Imelda Marcos' seven-count graft conviction over foundations tied to the Marcos family's Swiss accounts.

blocks.text: September 11, 2026 | 12:53pm

MANILA, Philippines — First family matriarch Imelda Marcos' latest acquittal raises an apparent contradiction: How could a graft conviction involving Swiss foundations collapse when courts have already ruled that hundreds of millions of dollars in Marcos Swiss deposits were ill-gotten?

The public release of the 2026 ruling in September was belated, having been handed down in June this year, but the ruling was clear on the lack of original documents and witnesses presented by the government. It adds to a pile of decades-old cases involving Marcos family members weakened due to evidentiary problems, particularly prosecutors' reliance on photocopied and unauthenticated documents or hearsay.

In 2007, the Regional Trial Court found authentication and hearsay issues in the prosecution's case, deciding to acquit Marcos for violations in overseas foreign-currency accounts and foreign exchange earnings.

In 2012, the Supreme Court similarly considered photocopies submitted by prosecutors as deficient evidence in establishing that Marcos' children—particularly politicians Bongbong Marcos and sister Imee—participated in accumulating ill-gotten wealth. Bongbong is now the president, while Imee is a senator.

In 2023, the high court similarly excluded unauthenticated documents from the pool of evidence in upholding the dismissal of a 2019 civil case on the alleged role of the Tantoco family acting as fronts for Marcoses. Imelda herself was accused of benefiting from duty-free shops' tax payments by diverted to foundations.

But the Swiss money itself has already been the subject of a separate and final ruling. In 2003, the Supreme Court ordered $658.2 million in Swiss deposits, plus interest, forfeited to the Philippine government as ill-gotten wealth. The accounts were held through foreign foundations, including several of the same entities mentioned in Imelda's more recent graft cases.

The court found that the deposits, which originally amounted to about $356 million, were far beyond Ferdinand and Imelda's known income of just $304,372.43 while they ruled over an authoritarian regime in the 1970s to 1980s. The Marcoses failed to show that the money had been lawfully acquired.
That ruling, however, was a civil forfeiture case. The criminal conviction of Imelda, which prosecutors attempted to push forward, was the case the high court decided on in June.
Why did the conviction fall through?
1. Records not properly authenticated

Most recently, the high court reversed the Sandiganbayan's 2018 ruling and acquitted the former first lady of seven violations of Section 3(h) of Republic Act 3019 for failure of the prosecution to prove her guilt beyond reasonable doubt.

Prosecutors failed to properly authenticate vital Swiss records and prove that the foundations qualified as "businesses" covered by the Anti-Graft and Corrupt Practices Act, the high court said in its ruling on June 10, 2026, but released only on Wednesday, September 9.

"The relevant Swiss documents were not properly authenticated," the Supreme Court said in its decision with Associate Justice Rodil Zalameda as ponente. "The prosecution was not able to present any credible witness who could have attested to the genuineness and due execution of the documents."

Former Solicitor General Francisco Chavez, former Philippine ambassador to Switzerland Luis Ascalon and a Presidential Commission on Good Government records officer could establish how the records came into government custody, the court said, but could not testify from personal knowledge about their contents or execution.
The court consequently treated the documents as inadmissible. It also ruled that their contents amounted to hearsay and lacked probative value even if they were considered admitted into evidence.
2. Foundations not proven to be businesses

The Supreme Court separately found that prosecutors failed to establish another key element of the offense: that the foundations in which Marcos allegedly held financial interests were "businesses" within the meaning of the anti-graft law.
The Sandiganbayan had treated activities such as maintaining bank accounts, transferring funds and earning investment returns as entrepreneurial activities.
But the high court found no evidence that the foundations regularly sold goods or services for profit.
"Just because the subject foundations may not be charitable does not mean that they are already businesses," the high court said.
It added that opening bank accounts, transferring money and earning interest or investment income "do not, by themselves, make an entity a commercial enterprise."

The court also faulted prosecutors for failing to present the applicable foreign laws needed to establish the legal character of the foundations. Several of the entities, including Maler, Trinidad, Rayby and Avertina, were organized under Liechtenstein law.
3. Wrong capacity alleged in four cases
The Supreme Court found an additional due process problem in four of the seven cases.
The Informations for the Maler, Trinidad, Rayby and Palmy foundations charged Marcos based on her position as a member of the Interim Batasang Pambansa.

The Sandiganbayan, however, convicted her based on a constitutional prohibition applicable to Cabinet members, who were barred under the 1973 Constitution from participating in the management of businesses.
The Supreme Court said the distinction mattered because different constitutional restrictions applied to the two positions.
Marcos could not be convicted in a capacity different from the one alleged against her, the court ruled, as doing so would violate her right to be informed of the nature and cause of the accusation.
2018 conviction reversed

What the Supreme Court reversed was the Sandiganbayan Fifth Division's conviction of Marcos in 2018 on seven graft counts involving Maler Establishment and the Trinidad, Rayby, Palmy, Vibur, Aguamina and Avertina foundations.
She was sentenced to six years and one month to 11 years in prison for each count and perpetually disqualified from holding public office.
The cases were among 10 graft charges filed against Marcos beginning in 1991. The Sandiganbayan acquitted her in the other three cases.

The Supreme Court stressed that its ruling concerns Marcos' criminal liability under the anti-graft law and does not determine whether the assets held through the foundations constitute ill-gotten wealth.
That question, the court said, belongs to separate civil forfeiture proceedings brought by the government.
"Ultimately, when the Court dons its robe, inclinations and personal beliefs are set aside, as they do not have a place in a court of law," the Supreme Court said.
It added that courts must decide cases based only on admissible and relevant evidence. — Camille Diola

articles.title: NSW police settle trespass case after visiting Indigenous children’s home 150 times in 20 months
articles.summary: Trespass case launched by two mothers settled after officers often went to families’ houses between midnight and 4am

blocks.text: Two Indigenous mothers have settled a trespass case against New South Wales police, after officers turned up at one of their homes 150 times in 20 months to conduct bail checks on her sons.
The case, which was launched against NSW police in April 2024, was settled on confidential terms three weeks before it was to go to trial in the supreme court.
One of the complainants, a single mum who uses the pseudonym Megan for privacy, has two sons, who were on bail from the ages of 11 and 13 after being found as passengers in a stolen car.
Police attended her home in regional NSW more than 150 times over 20 months, with many of the visits taking place between midnight and 4am.
NSW legislation allows courts to authorise police to attend a private residence to check that someone is complying with their bail conditions.
But the Justice and Equity Centre, representing Megan in court, argued that many of the bail checks were done without court authorisation, which amounted to trespass.
Megan said the visits often involved police banging on doors, shining torches through the windows and letting themselves in through the back gate in the middle of the night.
She said the visits were scary and stressful for her family and resulted in her kids missing school because of exhaustion.
‘‘My eldest is driving around with his head held high now, knowing police can’t just randomly pull him over,’’ Megan said.
‘‘But I know he’s still shaking in fear about what they could do.
‘‘They’ve already done the damage, and it will take a lot for my boys to start trusting police again.”
The other complainant, a single mum of three who uses the pseudonym Joanne, said police visited her western Sydney home to do bail checks on her son more than 90 times in 18 months.
She said in the space of a few hours, police conducted three such checks.
“The checks often happened on school nights, which meant my youngest daughter was too tired to go to school in the morning,” she said.
NSW police said the officers were acting lawfully when they conducted the bail compliance checks.
A police spokesperson said such checks were an important tool for keeping the public safe and managing risks associated with letting people out of jail during an ongoing court process.

But a report from the state’s Law Enforcement Conduct Commission, released in 2025, found police were stretching their authority and powers by relying on a weak legal principle to conduct bail compliance checks without court authorisation.
The mothers’ solicitor, Kate Sinclair, said it was immensely brave for her clients to bring the case against the force.
‘‘They did it for their families and their communities and we respect their courage,’’ she said.
Megan and her sons have separately taken NSW police to the federal court for racial discrimination, arguing that the boys were targeted because they are Aboriginal.
That case is ongoing.

articles.title: ‘I’m on the ticket’: Trump implores Republicans to vote in November at unusual midterm convention
articles.summary:
The president demonised Democrats in an attempt to wangle votes in midterms despite backlash over Iran war

With his approval rating at a historic low,

blocks.text: With his approval rating at a historic low, Donald Trump has brought down the curtain on the Republicans’ first ever midterm convention by pleading with supporters to do him “the biggest favour” and “pretend” they are voting for him in November’s US elections.

The president is facing a growing backlash over rising prices and the war in Iran. Sweeping losses for the Republican party could effectively turn Trump into a lame duck for his final two years in the White House.

Sensing political danger, Trump wrapped up the novel two-day event in Dallas, Texas, on Thursday with a pitch that critics are likely to say smacked of desperation: “You gotta do me the biggest favour you’ve ever done me. You’ve gotta do this for me. You’ve got to pretend I’m on the ticket. I’m on the ticket! I’m on the ticket! He’s on the ticket! Pretend I’m on the ticket because this is going to turn out to be one of the most important elections.”

In an improvised pledge of allegiance to himself, Trump directed the crowd of about 20,000 to raise their right hands and repeat: “I pledge to the greatest president in the history of the United States, that loves us so much he can’t even breathe, that I will go out with my family, my friends, I’ll do it any way – I don’t care if I’m registered or not, I’m going to try to cheat like hell like they do.”
The convention had been aimed at turning around Republicans’ fortunes. Opinion polls suggest they are on course to lose the US House of Representatives, and possibly the Senate.

In what was effectively an abridged version of his rambling keynote address on Wednesday, the president reiterated his promise of “Trump dividend” of $5,000 for every US adult if Republicans win both chambers of Congress. Democrats have dismissed the pledge as a bribe while economists have warned it would cost more than $1tn.
Trump also hammered the theme of the convention: drawing a contrast between his own accomplishments and what he argues amounts to a threat posed by Democrats.

“Less than two years ago, the American people gave us a mandate to save America – and in 19 months, I’ve delivered on every single promise I made,” he claimed. “They gave us wide open borders with 25 million people pouring in from all over the globe. They turned our cities into scenes of death and misery, murder, poverty and destruction, and made America a laughingstock all over world.
“But we took that dark age of America and turned it into the golden age of America.”

The reduction of prescription drug prices alone “should get us a big victory in our midterms”, he suggested, before he turned the microphone over to opera performer Christopher Macchio, who belted out a soaring rendition of America the Beautiful as red, white, blue and golden balloons cascaded down from the ceiling of the basketball arena.

The convention resembled a Trump mega-rally more than a traditional party meeting, with no nominations or formal business and more than 50 speakers or presentations each night. Supporters wore “Make America Great Again” regalia and waved signs displaying the Stars and Stripes. Republicans believe it has been successful in galvanising the party’s base in the face of stiff electoral headwinds.
Earlier on Thursday, speaker after speaker sought to champion Trump’s accomplishments while constantly branding the Democratic party as extremist and communist.
The president’s eldest son, Donald Trump Jr, delivered a fiery address setting Republican “common sense” against a “dystopian hellscape” of leftwing ideology.

“As we speak, Democrat candidates across the country are openly embracing the radical ideology of democratic socialism,” suggested Trump Jr. “They claim that their socialism is for the people, but that’s the exact same story we’ve heard from every communist in human history.”
Describing childhood memories of his grandparents in communist Czechoslovakia, he warned of bread lines and rationing. “Communism is on the march and it’s up to us to stop it in its tracks,” he said.

Trump Jr framed the Republican platform, including pledges to end taxes on tips, overtime and social security, as a direct response to a “war on the working people” by Democrats. “The choice is clear,” he said. “Don’t let these radicals gaslight you into thinking common sense is extreme, and extreme is somehow common sense. Don’t let them convince you that caring about this country makes you a villain.”
after newsletter promotion

Senator Ted Cruz meanwhile warned of a “red-green alliance” between “communists and Islamists” who “hate Christians, hate Jews and hate capitalism”. Invoking his father’s escape from Cuban communism, Cruz declared that “sharia law has no place in America” and is “fundamentally inconsistent with the constitution”.

The House speaker, Mike Johnson, echoed the conspiratorial tone, suggesting the nation was being “attacked from within”. The Democratic party is now beholden to radicals, he claimed, warning: “They’re the ones who have let the barbarians inside the gate, and next year the communists will be in Congress. That’s what’s so frightening.”

Johnson added that, while big names like Zohran Mamdani and Abdul El-Sayed are known entities, the bigger threat comes from “Democrats in the swing seats who say one thing, and then join forces and vote with the socialists that they’re afraid of”.

The US health secretary, Robert F Kennedy Jr, took the stage to champion the “Make America Healthy Again” (Maha) platform. The son of a former US attorney general and nephew of John F Kennedy said the “irony of my presence here is inescapable”.

He continued: “The Democrats of that era stood with labour and working people and the American middle class. Nearly every cop and firefighter was a Democrat … The Democratic party, in short, lost its way.”

Speaking less than a mile from the spot where his uncle was assassinated in 1963, Kennedy claimed it was a “fact” that “neither my father, nor my uncle, would recognise the Democratic party of today”.

JD Vance, the vice-president, gave the keynote address of the night. He said: “The Democrats are the party of hatred. They’re the party that despises America and the people who built it … America belongs to those who love it – not those who hate it.”
The political attacks were briefly paused for two sombre interludes.

A tribute marked one year since the assassination of rightwing provocateur and organiser Charlie Kirk. Lucas Miles, a Turning Point USA vice-president, said that while “they could take the man, they could not take the mission”. Chants of “Charlie, Charlie” filled the air.

The arena was plunged into darkness as Macchio performed Ave Maria on the eve of the 25th anniversary of the September 11 terrorist attacks. Two beams of light stretched upward from the arena floor, reminiscent of the twin towers in New York, as the crowd held up mobile phone lights. A video narration accompanying the tribute urged the audience to: “Say their names. Honour their sacrifice. Defend Freedom. Never forget September 11.”

Democrats have dismissed the Republican event as a stunt. At a press conference in Dallas, the congressman Robert Garcia, of California, told reporters: “What’s happening right now is Donald Trump is throwing a two-day party to celebrate himself, so that JD Vance can give a speech, and so his donors, some of whom have paid $800,000 a pop for these ticket packages, can spend two days celebrating themselves.

“This is happening as the American public is struggling. So as Donald Trump and JD Vance party away for two days, the average American family can’t afford groceries, the cost of the rent’s going up, they’re looking at their gas prices skyrocketing and they’re making difficult choices at the dinner table. But Donald Trump does not care about the average American family or about affordability.”

articles.title: $15m fund launched to create ‘unstoppable momentum’ to end FGM worldwide
articles.summary:
Her Horizon Fund seeks $100m to stop practice harming 230m women and girls globally

Frontline activists and leaders in the fight against female genital mutilation, which has affected more…

blocks.text: Frontline activists and leaders in the fight against female genital mutilation, which has affected more than 230 million women and girls worldwide, have welcomed an unprecedented $15.5m (£11.4m) fund aimed at creating “unstoppable momentum” to finally end the practice.

The launch of the fund comes as women’s rights are increasingly under attack and donor funding is in sharp decline, particularly for work led by FGM survivors in local communities. It is thought to be the largest single philanthropic contribution to ending the practice of FGM.
The United Nations has set a goal of elimination by by 2030, but progress is not on track as funding declines and legal protections are challenged.

Funding received by the largest initiative to end the practice – a joint programme operated in 18 countries by the UN’s sexual and reproductive health agency, UNFPA, and the UN humanitarian organisation for children, Unicef – fell by 45% last year, from $29.6m to $16.3m.
The Her Horizon Fund has been seeded with $14m from the Wallace Global Fund, plus an additional $1.5m contribution from an anonymous donor, making $15.5m in total.
The aim of Her Horizon Fund, set up by the US-based Wallace Global Fund, is to pool $100m from donors to reach a “tipping point” towards ending FGM within a generation.

Ifrah Ahmed, a Somali-Irish activist and survivor of FGM who set up the Ifrah Foundation to end practice in Somalia, where it is nearly universal, said: “By giving $14m, the global fund will ensure activists can continue their work in this area.”

UN funding worth $300,000 to her organisation was cut by UNFPA last year, but Ahmed managed to raise money from elsewhere. The Ifrah Foundation has helped push for anti-FGM legislation in Somalia, she said.

Three of Somalia’s seven federal member states have enacted anti-FGM laws, while in two other states bills banning the practice have been endorsed by cabinet and are awaiting parliamentary approval, albeit with opposition by religious leaders in some areas.
“If we don’t continue to raise money, the dream where this practice will end will have died for young girls,” she added.

Advocates warn that while international recognition of FGM as a human rights violation has grown, and countries such as Burkina Faso, the Gambia and Kenya have criminalised the practice, progress remains fragile.
In recent years, survivors and frontline groups have been trying to protect gains made over several decades.

The Gambia’s supreme court, for instance, is considering a constitutional challenge to the country’s 2015 ban on female genital mutilation and cutting. The case follows a 2024 parliamentary effort to repeal the ban, which lawmakers rejected after months of debate, amid strong resistance from women’s rights groups. In Sierra Leone, the new Child Rights Act does not prohibit FGM, despite sustained campaigning from rights groups.

Susan Gibbs, the Wallace Global Fund’s senior adviser on women’s rights and FGM, said: “Female genital mutilation is a global crisis, an extreme manifestation of gender-based violence and violence against children, and a public health emergency.

“There has been decades of progress, and UN data indicates declines in prevalence in a number of countries. But there have also been anti-rights pushback and political crises. Obviously, donor funding is in decline. So it’s a mixed picture.”
after newsletter promotion

She added: “We’re at this critical inflection point. Most frontline organisations have been absolutely starved for resources, and so more direct funding would allow them to sustain and scale [up] their work.”
Gibbs, who attended a Justice for Girls global gathering in Kenya earlier this month, where the fund was officially launched, said the momentum at the meeting was “incredible”.

“Lasting change must be led by the frontline – it cannot be imposed from the outside. Frontline survivors, activists, they know their communities and they know what it will take. They must have the resources and power to lead.
“I’m convinced the impact [of the fund] will be catalytic,” she said. “There’s no doubt in my mind that with adequate funding, these frontline activists have what it takes to get this done.”

FGM is the partial or total removal of female genitalia for non-medical reasons. It has been endured by more than 144 million women and girls in Africa, 80 million in Asia and 6 million in the Middle East. The practice can cause immediate health complications such as severe pain, excessive bleeding and infection, as well as long-term consequences that include complications during childbirth, chronic pain and lasting psychological trauma.
A 2025 study estimated that FGM causes approximately 44,000 deaths each year in the 15 countries examined, making it one of the leading causes of death for women and girls in those countries.

articles.title: JD Vance pitches himself as Trump’s political heir on day two of Republican midterm convention
articles.summary:
Vice-president dog-whistled, exaggerated claims of success and echoed Trump talking points to excited audience

JD Vance made a clear pitch that he should be the heir to

blocks.text: JD Vance made a clear pitch that he should be the heir to Donald Trump on Thursday night, closing out the Republicans’ midterm convention with a blistering speech that featured exaggerated claims of success, criticism of Democrats as “lunatics” and an aggressive dismissal of a protester waving a Mexican flag.

Speaking in Dallas, the vice-president showed he could channel the basest instincts of his boss, filling his remarks with dog whistles and echoing Trump’s false claims that Democrats “cheered” the 7 October massacre of Israelis.

Vance had been met with chants of “JD, JD,” as he walked on to the stage: the liveliest response anyone besides Trump received across the two-day convention, with some shouting that he should be the nominee in 2028.
“We gotta take care of business this November, then we’ll worry about what comes next,” the vice-president responded with a smile.

Vance began the speech by running through a list of Republican grievances, channeling Trump’s pugnacious attitude toward immigration as he told the crowd that two years ago “we were tired of being called racist for noticing that our country was becoming dirtier and poorer and less safe and less prosperous”.

The Make America Great Again (Maga) crowd inside the arena liked that line, but the loudest cheer of the night came when Vance responded to a protester who briefly interrupted his speech. Vance claimed the protester was waving a Mexican flag, and adopted a fiery tone as he said: “Well, my friend, if you love Mexico so much, get your ass over there I’ll buy you the plane ticket.”
The applause was rapturous.

The vice-president had to walk a tightrope coming into the speech, arguably the most important address of his short political career. He had to present his own case to the Republican base, without breaking too much from the notoriously sensitive Trump.
Vance praised Trump as “the toughest SOB in American politics”, and paused repeatedly as the crowd lavished him with cheers and applause.
He also invoked the recent birth of fourth child, saying he had been looking at “the future of this country through the eyes of the future of my son” and “the birthright of this newest of Americans”.
Addressing Democratic “radicals”, whom he accused of wanting to destroy the nuclear American family, he boomed: “Stay the hell away from our kids.”

But it was also a speech aimed squarely at rallying the Maga faithful: attacking transgender rights, extolling the importance of American manufacturing and religious freedom, and accusing Democrats of “doubling down on the crazy”.

Vance showed a penchant, too, for Trump’s baseless statements, claiming that some Democrats in New York “cheered on” the slaughter of Jewish people on 7 October, and suggesting that a “new generation” of Democrats seek to defund the police and “abolish the border”.

“What is it that drives this new generation of radical Democrats? It’s not new policies. They’ll say the same stuff: defund the police, abolish the border, the green new scam. We’ve heard all this stuff before,” Vance said. He then tried out a new line: “I think that what’s new about them is what motivates them is a new type of hardcore hatred.”

Vance won applause, too, for his praise of Charlie Kirk, the far-right activist who was assassinated in Utah exactly one year ago. Addressing Kirk’s children, who were not in the arena, Vance said: “History will record that your father was a great man.

“Those of us who loved your dad, we know him as something even better than a great man – he was a good man,” he added of Kirk, a man who, among other things, endorsed Trump’s stolen-election lies and the racist great replacement theory.
after newsletter promotion

One problem Vance could face should he run in 2028 is his attachment to the deeply unpopular Iran war, and foreign policy was conspicuous by its absence in his speech. Last week he rejected the use of the word “war”, but said he wouldn’t set “artificial lines” regarding an end to the conflict. The Wall Street Journal reported on Wednesday that Trump’s advisers have raised the prospect that the war could drag on through the rest of his term.
Vance did not address the war directly. But in an oblique reference he invoked Kirk’s disdain for conflict.
“Charlie hated war,” Vance said, before pleading with undecided voters to not abandon the party over policy differences.

“What I’m asking you to do is do what Charlie did: do not throw the baby out with the bathwater,” he said. “Don’t don’t give the country over to a bunch of crazy people because you happen to disagree with us on a policy issue here or there.”

A poll found Vance was the favorite choice among likely Republican primary voters, with 43% saying they wanted him to be the nominee in 2028. Marco Rubio, the secretary of state, got 21%; Donald Trump Jr was at 7%.

Vance will hope those numbers stick, but he wasn’t the only one auditioning in Dallas. Robert F Kennedy Jr, the health secretary who switched parties to support Trump in 2024, praised the president and attacked the Democratic party during a well-received speech earlier on Thursday, while Ted Cruz, the Texas senator, received a rousing response in his home state.

“They hate Christians, they hate Jews, they hate the ‌capitalism, they hate ⁠the constitution and they hate America,” Cruz said of Democrats, offering no evidence for his claims, but very much tapping into the theme of the two-day convention.

Rubio did not speak at the convention, instead taking part in a tour of South America. Both he and Cruz ran against Trump in 2016. During that contest, Trump dubbed Rubio “Little Marco” and suggested Cruz’s father was involved in the assassination of John F Kennedy.

Vance, by contrast, has never publicly attracted Trump’s ire, and he will want to keep it that way as he seeks to take on leadership of the party in two years’ time. That was likely the thinking as the vice-president ended his speech, shouting over jubilant applause that Trump was the “greatest president” before relinquishing the stage for his boss to bring the convention to a close.

articles.title: Hurricane Lowell knocks out key Hawaii port, disrupting food, fuel
articles.summary: HONOLULU — Crews began repairing the only cargo port on one of Hawaii’s smallest main islands while power was being restored to another island Thursday, two days after Hurricane Lowell skirted…

blocks.text: HONOLULU — Crews began repairing the only cargo port on one of Hawaii’s smallest main islands while power was being restored to another island Thursday, two days after Hurricane Lowell skirted along the state’s western edge. At least two deaths were linked to the storm.

On the island of Kauai, intense wind and surging waves damaged oceanfront resorts, ripped apart roads and knocked out power, prompting tourism officials to urge visitors to stay away for now. On Lanai, a harbor that supplies much of the food and fuel to its 3,300 residents was inoperable and will take about two weeks to repair, state officials said.

The overall destruction to Hawaii’s infrastructure, businesses and homes was expected to be the worst from a storm since Hurricane Iniki, a Category 4 storm that walloped Kauai in 1992 and caused $3 billion in damage.

While it has been a relatively quiet Atlantic hurricane season, there have been four hurricanes in the Pacific since the beginning of August. Another tropical storm formed Thursday, but it was not expected to make landfall.
Tourism takes a hit

Officials urged travelers to reschedule trips to Kauai or shift their destination to another island. Thousands of customers, including some resorts, remained without power, and crews continued clearing roads of downed trees and toppled utility poles.

“Adjusting your itinerary allows you to continue your Hawaiʻi vacation while supporting the state’s broader visitor economy as Kauaʻi recovers,” Caroline Anderson, interim president and chief executive officer of the Hawai‘i Tourism Authority, said in a statement.

Kauai sees only a small fraction of Hawaii’s almost 10 million visitors each year, but tourism is its top economic driver, with people coming from all over to take in its tropical landscapes, waterfalls and dramatic cliffs. Local estimates say tourism accounts for 4 out of every 10 jobs on the island.

The hurricane’s powerful storm surge buckled and washed away roads, knocked down the walls of homes and flooded resorts, sending rapids through a hotel lobby, overturning furniture and leaving debris everywhere. Extensive lines backed up at Kauai’s primary airport Thursday as people tried to depart the island.
Despite running a restaurant business, Kelly Kakalia, co-owner of The Musubi Truck, with three locations across Kauai, said she is not overly worried about the interruption to tourism.
“I would be silly to say tourism doesn’t drive our economy,” she said, but “our island needs time to rest and rebuild and make sure locals have power and water” before welcoming back tourists.
“If we take a little hit, that’s just part of it,” Kakalia said.
Governor asks Trump to declare a disaster
Democratic Gov. Joshn Green asked President Donald Trump on Wednesday to issue a major disaster declaration to expedite federal help for Kauai and Maui counties.
“We cannot wait for every damaged road, utility pole, harbor and public facility to be assigned a dollar value before asking the federal government to act,” Green said in making the request.
At Lanai’s main harbor, the storm opened a sinkhole, damaged part of the pier and scattered containers in the water, according to the state’s Transportation Department.

Planning was underway on other options to get supplies to the island, which sees only a few visitors. Billionaire Larry Ellison bought nearly all of the island in 2012 for about $300 million from the owner of agriculture and real estate company Castle & Cooke Inc.
First responders on Kauai’s south end found the body of a 74-year-old man Wednesday near the shoreline. Authorities believe his death was related to the storm surge, police said.
Another man was killed on Oahu when a large tree fell on his tent Monday during the storm, the governor said. The man was homeless and living in a park./dp

articles.title: Spanish lawmakers back citizenship for Sahrawis
articles.summary: Spanish lawmakers approved a bill that could give citizenship to tens of thousands of Sahrawis and their descendants, amid tense ties with Morocco. The legislation must now pass the senate.

image.caption: Tesh Sidi, the first woman of Sahrawi origin to serve in Spanish parliament, called for the adoption of the legislationImage: Susana Vera/REUTERS

blocks.text: Spanish lawmakers on Thursday voted to grant citizenship to people born in Western Sahara under Spanish colonization — a region now that is now largely controlled by Morocco.
The move could test Madrid's already delicate relations with Rabat, especially after the border crisis in Ceuta.
The lower house approved the bill by:

items: In favor: 168
Against: 31
Abstentions: 145

blocks.text: The legislation would grant Spanish nationality to Sahrawis born before September 29, 1977, and allow their descendants to obtain citizenship through naturalization.
Estimates of those eligible range from around 70,000 to more than 100,000.
The legislation must now pass the senate to become law.

blocks.caption: Many Sahrawis live in refugee camps in Tindouf, Algeria, or elsewhere abroad [FILE: February 25, 2025]Image: Juan Carlos Rojas/picture alliance

blocks.text: Morocco claims sovereignty over Western Sahara
Spain's ruling Socialist Party and its left-wing coalition partner Sumar supported the measure, while the conservative People's Party abstained and far-right Vox opposed it.

Sumar lawmaker Tesh Sidi, the first woman of Sahrawi origin to serve in parliament, said the legislation restores the "Spanish national identity card to those Sahrawis who once held ​and from whom this state took it away."
Spain controlled Western Sahara until 1976. Morocco claims sovereignty over the territory, while an indigenous resistance group, the Polisario Front, seeks independence.

Morocco occupies almost all of the territory. Meanwhile, the Polisario Front across the border in the Algerian town of Tindouf, where tens of thousands of displaced Saharawi people live in refugee camps.
The region remains on the United Nations' list of non-self-governing territories.
How the Ceuta influx raised tensions
The vote comes amid renewed tensions between Madrid and Rabat following a large influx of migrants into Spain's North African enclave of Ceuta in July.
Scores of migrants died in their attempt to reach EU territory, most by drowning.
Western Sahara dispute: Morocco's gamble won global support
Although most of those who breached Ceuta's borders have returned, thousands remain, many of them unaccompanied minors living in dire conditions.
The incident caused a major rift among EU member states, most publicly between Spain's left-wing government and Italy's far-right leadership.

articles.title: New York marks 25th anniversary of 9/11 attacks
articles.summary: NEW York, United States – New York commemorates the 25th anniversary of the devastating September 11, 2001 attacks Friday with a ceremony marked by US President Donald Trump’s absence and…

blocks.text: NEW York, United States – New York commemorates the 25th anniversary of the devastating September 11, 2001 attacks Friday with a ceremony marked by US President Donald Trump’s absence and right-wing outrage at the attendance of the city’s first Muslim mayor.
Trump will pay his respects at the Pentagon, not New York, where hijacked planes destroyed the World Trade Center and killed most of the 2,977 total victims on that world-altering day.

Vice President JD Vance and Trump’s four living predecessors – Republican George W. Bush, who was in office during the attacks, and Democrats Joe Biden, Barack Obama and Bill Clinton – are all expected at the “Ground Zero” site in lower Manhattan.
No one will give speeches at the ceremony, while bereaved family members will read out the names of all of those killed and a bell rung to mark major moments during the attack.

“Memorials like this and discussions about those events are an important part of keeping it alive and understanding how we prevent tragedies like this from ever happening again,” said Robert Kafka, a Chicagoan in his 60s visiting the 9/11 Memorial.

Alongside the former presidents will be Democratic Mayor Zohran Mamdani, the Big Apple’s first Muslim mayor, despite a campaign urging him to stay away spearheaded by the right-wing New York Post and former mayor Rudy Giuliani.

A petition, which has gathered more than 100,000 signatures, accuses Mamdani of associating with unspecified individuals who are “dismissive of American institutions or insufficiently critical of extremist ideologies.”
“It’s concerning to me that the mayor is being treated differently simply because he is Muslim,” city council member Shahana Hanif told CNN.
Mamdani won plaudits however for recently revealing thousands of documents showing what city officials knew about toxicity levels of the air in Lower Manhattan following the attacks.

After the initial dust cloud that followed the collapse of the World Trade Center, months of pollution and lingering dust ensued, causing cancers from which thousands of New Yorkers still suffer today.
Toxic air
“People got sick because the leaders they trusted lied and told them they were safe to breathe in toxic air,” Mamdani said Tuesday.
Nineteen Al-Qaeda operatives hijacked four planes on that nearly cloudless day in 2001. Two jets slammed into the World Trade Center’s Twin Towers, causing the iconic 110-story buildings to collapse.
A third plane struck the Pentagon, while a fourth crashed into a field near Shanksville, Pennsylvania, after passengers fought back.
Beyond those killed on September 11, more than 9,400 other people have died from 9/11-related illnesses, according to the federal program established to provide medical care to those affected.
Some 100 million Americans were not even born or are too young to remember the tragic events.
Logan Miller, 32, lost his uncle during the attacks, and his grandfather to 9/11-related illness in the aftermath.
“I think the next generation just can’t fathom what actually transpired and how someone could be impacted by that, and so I actually find them asking more questions,” he told AFP.
Huge crowds are expected to gather in Lower Manhattan for the memorial service.
The Secret Service has erected a security ring of steel around the site of the 9/11 Memorial and Museum.
Police commissioner Jessica Tisch said an anti-drone team would be deployed as a precaution, but stressed there was no intelligence of a specific threat to the gathering.
Al-Qaeda meanwhile has marked the anniversary by releasing a video showing images of late leader Osama bin Laden and his son Hamza, who Trump said in 2019 had also been killed.
Ahead of the memorial, a drone show with 2,977 lights rose above New York Harbor, one for each person killed in the attacks./dp

articles.title: Hastie accepts apology from Joyce over ‘traitor’ cartoon as Hanson doubles down and tells critics to ‘chill’
articles.summary:
A split emerges in One Nation over the video, with Barnaby Joyce offering an apology as Pauline Hanson continues to refuse to take down the video

Andrew Hastie has accepted an apology from…

blocks.text: Andrew Hastie has accepted an apology from his former colleague Barnaby Joyce over a One Nation cartoon video labelling the former SAS captain a traitor but reiterated that he believed Pauline Hanson was a “lying coward”.

The apology has revealed a split between Joyce and his leader, as Hanson instead appeared to double down on the controversial animation on social media, thanking Hastie for drawing attention to the video posted more than one month ago and saying critics should “take a chill pill”.

Hastie had called on Hanson and One Nation to take ownership of the cartoon or remove it from social media, after the One Nation leader said she personally had not called the Liberal frontbencher a traitor.
The One Nation video posted to social media in late July depicts Hastie as a pitiful and paranoid opposition leader manipulated by Anthony Albanese into taking on One Nation.
It also refers to him being a traitor after he gave evidence against the Victoria Cross-winner Ben Roberts-Smith in his failed defamation trial.
Joyce quickly distanced himself from the video on Wednesday, saying he was not aware it. He later told the press he had reached out to Hastie.
On Friday Hastie told Guardian Australia he accepted Joyce’s explanation.
“Barnaby Joyce has reached out to me and explained that he didn’t know about the cartoon that called me a traitor eight times,” Hastie said. “I accept his explanation.
“I called him a lying coward because I thought he was protecting Pauline Hanson. I now know that she is the only lying coward.”
Hastie has accused Hanson of being “weak” and having a “glass jaw” and said the video not only insults him but all veterans, including others who gave evidence at the defamation trial.
Hanson has refused to apologise or pull down the video and has taken aim at critics including Jacqui Lambie, who backed Hastie and called the One Nation leader an “angry little woman”.
She posted a photo of Lambie on X and wrote: “I think everyone needs to take a chill pill.” The video remained pinned to the top of her X account on Friday.
Joyce would not weigh into whether the video should be taken down, telling News24 on Thursday night it was “beyond my pay grade”.
“I’m not responsible for putting the cartoons up and I’m not responsible for taking them down,” he MP said. “So, you know, it’s an odd discussion for me.

“If I believe a person’s hurt and I listen to it and I think, no, that’s fair enough, you’re not a traitor, therefore if you feel hurt by that because you think it’s too close to the bone, even though it’s a cartoon, I’m not making excuses because it’s a cartoon, but it wasn’t actually said by anybody in One Nation to him then nonetheless, it should be apologised for, so I apologise.”
But the One Nation senator Sean Bell said it was a “shame” Hastie had decided to make the issue about himself.

“I don’t think the party has anything to apologise for,” he told News24. “I think people should go and watch the cartoon, because I think, in it, there’s a lot of very insightful things, because it’s not just about Mr Hastie, it’s about the Liberal party as a whole. It’s about the Labor party and some of the tricks they use.
“Mr Hastie’s has been looking to have a fight and a conflict with One Nation for a long, long time.”
Senior Liberals, Lambie, the RSL and the Greens have all criticised the video, and pushed for it to be taken down.
On Friday the defence minister and deputy prime minister, Richard Marles, said the use of the word traitor was “tasteless”.

“Andrew Hastie is definitely not a traitor,” he told ABC radio. “I know him well and I’ve said this publicly. I very much honour the service that Andrew Hastie has given to our country, wearing our nation’s uniform. I think to use that word in respect of a veteran is extremely tasteless.
“No one should be using that word in respect of any veteran and in respect of Andrew.”

articles.title: More Tiananmen vigil activists sentenced to prison in Hong Kong security case
articles.summary: A Hong Kong court sentenced three activists — who for years organized vigils in remembrance of China's 1989 Tiananmen Square crackdown — to prison for terms ranging from five to more than seven years…

image.caption: Lee Cheuk-yan, middle, and Albert Ho, far right, along with Chow Hang-tung were sentenced in a Hong Kong court Friday. (Tyrone Siu/Reuters)

blocks.text: World·New

A Hong Kong court sentenced three activists — who for years organized vigils in remembrance of China's 1989 Tiananmen Square crackdown — to prison for terms ranging from five to more than seven years on Friday in a case that is widely seen as a barometer of the city's freedoms as Beijing clamps down on dissent.
The 3 activists were convicted under a Beijing-imposed national security law
Lee Cheuk-yan, Chow Hang-tung and Albert Ho were convicted of inciting subversion earlier this year under a Beijing-imposed national security law.

Lee and Chow, who pleaded not guilty, received prison terms of seven years, and seven years plus three months. Ho was given five years plus two months, lower than his co-defendants partly because of his guilty plea.
The trio of defendants was charged in September 2021 and has been held in custody for years.
Hong Kong once had a vibrant civil society marked by massive protests and a freewheeling press scene.

For three decades, the vigil was the only large-scale, public commemoration in China that drew tens of thousands of people annually. It symbolized the civil liberties Hong Kong enjoyed under Beijing's "one country, two systems" governing principle after Britain handed the former colony back to China in 1997.

items: Hong Kong pro-democracy activist Joshua Wong pleads guilty in 2nd national security case
Tiananmen Square vigil organizers convicted of 'inciting subversion' in Hong Kong

blocks.text: But after a 2019 protest movement rocked the city, authorities reduced public choice in elections and prosecuted leaders of news outlets known for their critical reports of the government. Many leading activists were imprisoned under the security law, and dozens of civil society groups dissolved, including the alliance.
Beijing says the law is necessary to maintain stability.
The sentences for the Tiananmen activists are the latest high-profile penalties imposed under the security law.
In February, former pro-democracy media tycoon Jimmy Lai was sentenced to 20 years in prison.

articles.title: 'It was heartbreaking'- Americans remember what they were doing on 9/11
articles.summary: The BBC asks people in Washington what they were doing on that day and how 11 September 2001 changed the country.

blocks.text: On Tuesday 11 September 2001, hijackers seized US passenger jets and crashed them into two New York skyscrapers, killing thousands of people.
A third plane destroyed the western face of the Pentagon - the giant headquarters of the US military just outside the nation's capital, Washington DC.
The fourth plane crashed in a field in Pennsylvania after passengers fought back. It is thought the hijackers had meant to attack Washington's Capitol Building.

articles.title: Man flees road rage incident near Vancouver that ended with him being chased with a knife
articles.summary: Robin Nuber was in Los Angeles on the weekend, but it was after he returned home to British Columbia that he found himself in a scene he likened to an "action movie," speeding in reverse to escape a…

image.caption: Robin Nuber can be heard telling the man who was fleeing to 'hold on' to his car as he distanced it from the man with a knife. (Submitted by Robin Nuber)

blocks.text: British Columbia

Robin Nuber was in Los Angeles on the weekend, but it was after he returned home to British Columbia that he found himself in a scene he likened to an "action movie," speeding in reverse to escape a man with a knife who was chasing a frightened victim clinging to the outside of Nuber's Tesla.
Victim sustained multiple injuries, including cuts, a bloody mouth and a gouged-eye, says witness

"I just got back, so I literally felt like I was at Universal Studios where they do the staged remakes of movies, and everything's kind of like an action movie," the Surrey, B.C., photographer said on Thursday
"It felt like I was at an actual movie set, but nope, it was not — it was very real."

Nuber had been heading to a photo shoot in Redwood Park in Surrey on Wednesday when he encountered the scene of a man with a knife clambering over a pickup truck in pursuit of another man, who ran toward Nuber's Tesla.
A video captured by Nuber's vehicle shows the assailant chasing the car as it reverses away, the other man hanging onto an open back door as Nuber tries to put distance between them and the pursuer.
Nuber can be heard telling the victim to "hold on" before the vehicle stops and the man climbs inside when they are far enough away from the attacker.
He said the victim suffered multiple injuries, including a bloody mouth, gouged right eye and cuts on an arm.
Surrey police said a 37-year-old man was facing multiple charges, including assault with a weapon, criminal harassment and uttering threats and he remained in custody.
He was due in Surrey Provincial Court on Thursday to set a next appearance date.
"The victim attempted to drive away in his Ford pickup truck when the suspect drove his Jeep Wrangler into it," Surrey police said in a statement on Thursday.

"The victim then ran from the truck as the suspect allegedly brandished a knife and chased after him. Fortunately, a nearby witness driving a Telsa provided the victim safety until SPS officers arrived.

items: Cat in the Hat suspect who chased a teen girl in B.C. appears to be a trend copycat
North Vancouver road rage dispute over merging leaves 1 in critical condition: police

blocks.text: The statement said several police officers were called to the scene at about 4:44 p.m. and took the suspect into custody without incident.
Nuber said he had turned up at a parking lot when he saw a pickup truck and a Jeep had collided, with both cars' airbags deployed.
"I thought that it might be a road rage incident. So, I slowed my car down, and then I took my phone out and started to film what started to happen," said Nuber.
Then he heard someone yelling "he's got a knife.'
The chase ensued after a man with no shoes ran toward him, shouting for help.
"The guy basically ended up hanging onto my car and then being kind of dangled underneath the door for about 100 feet. I think I dragged him just to get him away from the guy," Nuber said.
"And then eventually he kind of begged me to stop the car so he could get inside because he was obviously getting road rash."
Nuber said the suspect gave up the chase, walked to the woods and threw the knife into the forest, before police arrived minutes later.
He said the incident was a test of his survival instincts.
"I think if you ever face a situation, you might be impressed with yourself, with what your instincts do," said Nuber.

articles.title: QC court defers Sara Duterte's arraignment as VP calls Marcos an 'addict'
articles.summary: The Quezon City Regional Trial Court deferred on Friday, September 11, the arraignment of Vice President Sara Duterte for her grave threats charge after a motion filed by her camp.

blocks.text: September 11, 2026 | 10:44am
Philippine Vice President Sara Duterte (C) talks to her supporters after posting bail at a court building in Quezon City suburban Manila on September 5, 2026.
AFP / Ted Aljibe

MANILA, Philippines — The Quezon City Regional Trial Court deferred on Friday, September 11, the arraignment of Vice President Sara Duterte for her grave threats charge after a motion filed by her camp.
The court ordered the Department of Justice (DOJ) to comment on the motion before it rules, Duterte's lawyer Paul Lawrence Lim told reporters.
Until then, Duterte will not be formally read the charges or asked to enter a plea.
Duterte's lawyer declined to disclose the contents of the motion.
The DOJ, in a statement, said it respects the court's decision to postpone the arraignment pending a resolution of the motion by the defense.
"We will allow the judicial process to take its course. At this point, the prosecution will reserve further comment until the motion has been resolved," it said.
The department declined to comment on the nature of Duterte's motion.
Duterte went to the Quezon City Regional Trial Court in person on Friday, where she fired up a crowd of supporters in her calls for President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. to step down.
"Umalis ka diyan! Sinungaling ka! Abusado ka!" she said, addressing Marcos. (Get out of there! You're a liar! You're abusive!)
She accused Marcos of bringing "nothing but hardship" to Filipinos and called him an "addict," a familiar refrain that her father, former President Rodrigo Duterte, also hurled at Marcos.
"That's how it is with addicts. Their thinking is no longer grounded in reality," she said in Filipino.
"Remember, we will keep calling for the departure of our country's problem, whose name is Bongbong Marcos," she said.
Duterte thanked the crowd for skipping work "just to show the whole world the abusive nature of the administration."
"Our fight is not on social media, because our enemy is inside government buildings," she said.

The case against Duterte stems from a November 2024 briefing, where she said she had hired someone to kill Marcos, First Lady Liza Araneta-Marcos and then-House Speaker Martin Romualdez if she herself were killed.
The charges were filed in relation to Republic Act 10175, or the Cybercrime Prevention Act.
The DOJ filed the case on August 11.
On September 4, a Quezon City court found probable cause to try Duterte, ordered her arrest and set bail at P120,000 per count.
Duterte appeared before the court and posted P360,000 in cash bail on September 5.
Duterte's lawyers argue that the trial court has no jurisdiction over the case, saying the 1987 Constitution gives impeachable officials limited procedural immunity while in office.
The Quezon City court already rejected her bid to quash the charges on jurisdictional grounds before it issued the arrest warrant.
In her petition before the Supreme Court, Duterte argued that prosecuting her while she is vice president is an illegal way of removing her from office without an impeachment conviction.

articles.title: Former Carlton president apologises to ex-wife as lewd photo defamation case settles
articles.summary:
Luke Sayers says he accepts Cate Sayers did not post photo of his genitals as she says settlement closes ‘painful and difficult chapter’

Embattled former AFL club president Luke Sayers has…

blocks.text: The embattled former AFL club president Luke Sayers has apologised to his former wife for the harm he caused as her defamation case over a lewd photo settled.
Lawyers for Sayers, the immediate past president of the Carlton football club, read out the apology in the Victorian supreme court on Friday after indicating the settlement.
“I acknowledge the extreme hurt and harm caused to Cate Sayers by suggesting she posted or may have posted [the lewd photo],” the barrister Sandip Mukerjea said on behalf of Sayers.
“I accept she did not do this. To the extent I may have suggested otherwise, I apologise unreservedly to her.”

Cate Sayers had claimed Luke Sayers had defamed her in a statutory declaration, which accused her of accessing his X account, posting a photograph of his genitals in January 2025 and tagging a female executive at Bupa.
The document was sworn by Luke Sayers in the weeks after the controversial post, which was quickly deleted, as the AFL and Carlton conducted investigations.
In May, Luke Sayers, a former PwC chief executive, applied to have the case transferred to the federal circuit and family court of Australia where the matter would be heard in private.
But Justice Andrew Watson rejected the application in June, finding the supreme court was the more appropriate venue for a defamation claim.
The judge on Friday dismissed the proceedings and commended the parties for reaching the settlement, the terms of which were not discussed in open court.
“All litigation involves time, expense and risk,” Watson said. “There was every reason to expect this proceeding would be no different.”
Outside court, Cate Sayers said she accepted her ex-husband’s apology and the settlement closed a “painful and difficult chapter” for her.
“I commenced these proceedings to establish the truth, clearly and finally,” she told reporters. “With Luke’s apology, I feel I have achieved what I set out to do.”
She thanked the women who had supported her and said she hoped Friday’s outcome gave them the strength to stand up for the truth.
She added that said she wanted to move forward with her life and did not confirm whether the settlement included a monetary component.
Luke Sayers chaired the Carlton board from 2021 to 2025. Before that, he headed consultancy firm PwC Australia between 2012 and 2020.
At an inquiry into a confidentiality and tax scandal in 2023, he apologised while stating he had no knowledge of it during his tenure.
“If the [tax office] had directly and formally advised me as the CEO of PwC Australia ... I would have sought details and ensured a full and thorough investigation,” he said at the time.

articles.title: 'Nothing happens here. You're safe': 9/11 survivors, responders recall attack aftermath
articles.summary: Pilots, politicians, hotel workers, bus drivers and church leaders who had a front row seat to the aftermath of the Sept, 11, 2001, terrorist attacks gathered at the Gander airport on Thursday to…

image.caption: An evening of 'untold stories' from the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks was held at the Gander airport on Thursday night. Among those sharing their experiences were, from left, Gambo bus driver Frazer Lush, former federal transport minister David Collenette and Gander hospitality worker Lana Andre

blocks.text: Nfld. & Labrador·New

Pilots, politicians, hotel workers, bus drivers and church leaders who had a front row seat to the aftermath of the Sept, 11, 2001, terrorist attacks gathered at the Gander airport on Thursday to reflect on a life-changing experience.
Nearly 7,000 bewildered and scared passengers were stranded in Gander in the aftermath
David Collenette was addressing an audience in Montreal on the morning of Sept. 11, 2001.
At the time, the veteran Ontario politician was the federal minister of transport in the Liberal government of Jean Chrétien.
He began noticing some unusual rumblings in the audience, and then an aide walked up to him while he was speaking and presented him with a blunt note: "Wind up your speech. There's been a tragedy."
Passenger jets had been hijacked and were slamming into the World Trade Center towers in New York, the Pentagon in Washington, and a field in Pennsylvania.

As he scrambled back to Ottawa, Collenette was forced to make decisions that will forever be remembered in aviation history, including ordering 229 passenger jets bound for the United States to land immediately at Canadian airports, including those in Gander, St. John's, Stephenville and Happy Valley-Goose Bay.
Then, he ordered everyone to remain on the planes for hours until officials could be sure there were no more security threats.
"I think we made the right decisions," Collenette said during an event at Gander International Airport Thursday evening called "Untold Stories — Reconnected."

Hundreds of people gathered there to hear Collenette and others reflect on their experiences of the Sept. 11 attacks on the eve of the 25th anniversary of one of the most defining and catastrophic events in modern history. Just under 3,000 people were killed.

On that day, 38 commercial airliners touched down in Gander after North American airspace was closed in response to the attacks — delivering nearly 7,000 bewildered and scared passengers and crew to the central Newfoundland town, and effectively doubling Gander's population in a matter of hours.

The sudden arrival sparked a humanitarian response by area towns that inspired the hit musical Come From Away, and forged a unique and lasting bond between the stranded passengers and those who cared for them.

Thursday night's guest speakers included three of the pilots who landed their planes in Gander. One of them, Guy Gullick, was at the controls of US Airways Flight 3 from Rome to Philadelphia — the last plane to land in Gander that day.
'What kindness, compassion and humanity looks like'
After landing, Gullick wondered why there wasn't any security around the planes, an issue he raised when an airport employee boarded his jet.
Gullick said he'll never forget the answer to a very serious question: "He said, 'nothing happens here. You're safe."

It set the tone for the next several days, as passengers and air crews say they were treated to a level of hospitality and support that shocked and heartened those whose travel plans were upended by the attacks.
Gullick made special mention of hospitality worker Susan Scharpegge, who worked long hours and "slept on the floor" at the hotel "while we had rooms."
"You showed the world what kindness, compassion and humanity looks like," said Gullick. "You're an example for the world, and the world needs that right now."
Salvation Army officer Marlene George was among the responders and recalled encountering a worried and confused passenger.
George told the passenger that, "if you have to be stranded anywhere in the world, you landed in the right place."
She said area residents responded with "genuine love" to the so-called "plane people."
Striking school bus driver and Gambo resident, Frazer Lush, was among those who abandoned their picket lines to land a hand.
"It's not about a strike or a job. It's about helping people who needed us," said Lush, who also helped clean schools that had become emergency shelters.
Collenette, meanwhile, recalled the urgency he faced that day, with a plane entering Canadian airspace every 90 seconds and worries that one, or more, of them may pose a threat.
"We all had a job to do, and we reacted instinctively," he said. "Let's hope it doesn't happen again."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Terry Roberts is a reporter with CBC Newfoundland and Labrador, based in St. John’s. He previously worked for the Telegram, the Compass and the Northern Pen newspapers during a career that began in 1991. He can be reached by email at Terry.Roberts@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Sara Duterte expected to attend arraignment in grave threats case
articles.summary: Vice President Sara Duterte is expected to attend her arraignment before the Quezon City Regional Trial Court on Friday, September 11.

blocks.text: September 11, 2026 | 8:29am

Philippine Vice President Sara Duterte (L) walks with one of her lawyers Paul Lim (R) as she arrives at a court building to post bail in Quezon City suburban Manila on September 5, 2026, after a warrant of arrest was issued. A Philippine court on September 4 issued an arrest warrant for Vice President Sara Duterte over an alleged death threat against the country's president, with her defence team saying she would "exercise all her legal remedies".
AFP / Ted Aljibe
MANILA, Philippines — Vice President Sara Duterte is expected to attend her arraignment before the Quezon City Regional Trial Court on Friday, September 11.
Duterte is scheduled to appear at 8 a.m. Friday at the Quezon City Hall of Justice for her arraignment, her spokesperson lawyer Salvador Paolo Panelo Jr. confirmed on Thursday, September 10.

The vice president is facing three counts of grave threats over her remarks against President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos Jr., First Lady Liza Araneta-Marcos and former House Speaker Martin Romualdez.
The charges stemmed from an online press briefing in November 2024, when Duterte said she had hired someone to kill the Marcos couple and Romualdez if she herself were killed.
The Quezon City court issued an arrest warrant against Duterte on September 4 after finding probable cause to hold her for trial. The warrant was served by police at the Office of the Vice President.
Duterte posted bail the following day at Quezon City RTC Branch 98, which was the assigned weekend court.
The court set bail at P120,000 for each count, or P360,000 in total. It later lifted the arrest warrant after Duterte's lawyers submitted the required documents.
During Friday's arraignment, the charges will be formally read to Duterte, after which she will be asked to enter a plea for each of the three counts.
If she pleads not guilty, the case will proceed toward trial and the court may set the next hearings.

Duterte's legal team has questioned the court's jurisdiction over the case. Her lawyers also argued that impeachable officials have limited procedural immunity while in office under the 1987 Constitution.
The court heard oral arguments on Duterte's motion to quash in late August.
The Department of Justice, however, maintained that there is prima facie evidence with reasonable certainty of conviction to support the three charges.
On Monday, Duterte's lawyers asked the Supreme Court to resolve her application for a temporary restraining order in the grave threats case before the Quezon City court.

The case is being heard as Duterte faces an impeachment trial before the Senate. The alleged threats against Marcos also form part of one of the Articles of Impeachment against the vice president. — with a report from Ian Laqui

articles.title: Cat in the Hat suspect who chased a teen girl in B.C. appears to be a trend copycat
articles.summary: A disturbing incident in which someone dressed in a Cat in the Hat costume chased a teenager in West Kelowna, B.C., occurred amid an online trend that twists the popular children's character into…

image.caption: B.C. RCMP spokesperson Staff Sgt. Kris Clark says police were already aware of the trend ahead of the Aug. 24, 2026, incident. (West Kelowna RCMP)

blocks.text: British Columbia

A disturbing incident in which someone dressed in a Cat in the Hat costume chased a teenager in West Kelowna, B.C., occurred amid an online trend that twists the popular children's character into something sinister, leading police in some jurisdictions to warn of offline consequences.
Police warn that threatening posts can have real consequences
· The Canadian Press
· Posted: Sep 10, 2026 7:25 PM EDT | Last Updated: 10 minutes ago

While the incident in the Okanagan region last month happened in real life and has triggered an RCMP investigation, the Cat in the Hat social media trend typically involves generative AI depictions of the character and his distinctive red-and-white striped hat standing outside schools, homes or other locations.
Posts include TikTok videos with thousands of views showing the character in front of B.C. secondary schools or malls.
Other posts have included the names of individuals and their schools along with onscreen text such as "see you soon" or "bye bye."
With captions like "watch out," and "you're next," the unsettling images are leading police to warn the posts may have real world consequences if taken too far.

items: B.C. teen girl chased by Cat in the Hat amid online trend
RCMP say they arrested youth east of Ottawa because of potential threat

blocks.text: This week the Nechako Lakes school district in B.C.'s central Interior said it was aware of the social media trend and asked community members to report the posts to police.

B.C. RCMP spokesman Staff Sgt. Kris Clark said police were aware of the trend, including a case in Fort St. James in the Nechako Lakes school district, as well as the West Kelowna incident on Aug. 24 that was described by police on Tuesday.
Clark said he was "not aware of any other events in B.C. RCMP jurisdictions."
The criminality
Regarding criminality, "it would depend on the totality of the circumstances and whether sufficient evidence existed before an assessment for charge approval could be made," he said.

"Generally speaking, based on what I have seen, some potential offences could be uttering threats or criminal harassment; however, there are any number of others that may be considered depending on the available evidence."

West Kelowna RCMP had said last month's "concerning prank" may constitute criminal harassment, and other charges such as assault, uttering threats or intimidation could be considered if the evidence supported them.

"Regardless of whether the individual intended the behaviour as a joke, following a young person and causing them to fear for their safety is extremely concerning," Cpl. Devon Gerrits said in a statement, which included a photo of the character taken at night.
“People should understand that behaviour intended as a prank can have serious consequences when it causes another person to reasonably fear for their safety.”

Police in Tennessee, meanwhile, have said a student was arrested for making threats against school property with an AI-generated Cat in the Hat post and a teenager in Colorado was charged with harassment for a similar post that implied the character would appear outside a middle school and homes.

The Cat in the Hat character first appeared in the book of the same name by Theodor "Dr. Seuss" Geisel in 1957, but the costumed version from the videos is seemingly inspired by the 2003 live-action movie starring Canadian actor Mike Myers.
A viral post about the costume from the movie going up for auction may have sparked the horror-inspired trend, with some commenters describing it as uncanny and "nightmare fuel."

articles.title: Ukraine's fortress cities under fire as Russia bids to seize rest of Donbas
articles.summary: Kramatorsk and Slovyansk are now the main focus of Russian ground assaults, and residents are being told to leave.

blocks.text: It is so dangerous now in Slovyansk and Kramatorsk that police say it is time for civilians to get out. These neighbouring cities are the biggest still under full Ukrainian control in the eastern Donbas region.
In the worst affected areas, forced evacuations of families with children have already begun, says Pavlo Dyachenko of Donetsk police.
"This is the only way to save your life," he says, because security has deteriorated so much.
"If you take Slovyansk, it used to be hit by glide bombs roughly once a week, but now it's almost every day."
Slovyansk, Kramatorsk and Kostyantynivka, to the south, form part of what is known as Ukraine's "fortress belt" – a system of heavily reinforced defence lines in the east.
However, Kostyantynivka only has a limited presence of Ukrainian troops left, reports say, while Russia claims to be in full control of it.
Over the summer, the number of civilians wounded by Russian attacks on the two cities increased from 70 in June to 212 in August, say Ukrainian police.
Sixteen people died in June, 20 in July and 15 in August.
Residential housing comes under attack as well as infrastructure, says Dyachenko, causing "very significant destruction".
The number of glide bombs launched by Russia jumped from 40 in June to 109 in July and 92 in August, according to data published by Ukrainian police and studied by the BBC.
One morning two weeks ago, on 25 August, nine glide bombs targeted Kramatorsk. Seven hit civilian apartment blocks, wounding 24 people including a two-month-old baby, Ukrainian police say.
Two days later, it was hit again, this time with seven glide bombs, and five bombs targeted Slovyansk.
Fitted with winglets so they can glide to their target rather than fall, glide bombs are considered one of the most effective and lethal weapons in Russia's arsenal.
Usually, they weigh 250 or 500 kg, but there have been cases of Russia deploying bombs that weigh 1,500 kg.
"The devastation they cause is simply incredible," says Dyachenko.
"Glide bombs are the big fear," another British volunteer, John Auckland Abbey, posted on social media.

"They are silent killers, and when you've been abruptly woken by one exploding, you know at least another one will follow. The question you ask yourself as you lie very still in the dark is: will the next one be closer?"
Kramatorsk is currently home to the headquarters of the Donetsk regional administration. The capital city used to be Donetsk, until it was captured in 2014 by Russian-backed separatists.

What happens to the areas of Donbas still under Ukrainian control was reportedly a key issue when US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner visited Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky last weekend after their talks with Putin.
In the past, Witkoff has appeared to back Russian claims to the region, but Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky is refusing to pull troops out of it.
He says Putin has given his generals until the end of the year to complete their occupation of Donbas.
"Putin's primary objective on the front line remains the same: Kostyantynivka-Slovyansk," Zelensky told journalists last month.

Faced with mounting military pressure, the Ukrainian leader has created two new taskforces headed by experienced generals, Andriy Biletsky and Denys Prokopenko, to defend the portion of Donbas still in Ukrainian hands.
"There isn't just a battle for Donbas there," one unnamed Ukrainian general has said.
"What is probably the main battle of this year and the next is now unfolding."
